briefing: This week’s evidence indicates that graphene and related two-dimensional materials are increasingly being engineered as functional interfaces rather than standalone materials. Across photonics, sensing, energy storage and flexible electronics, performance gains are linked to confinement, contact design, conductive coatings and hybrid architectures, with several results still at laboratory or preclinical stage. The First Graphene–Aeropreg agreement stands out as a commercialization signal, suggesting composite integration may be nearer-term than many device and biomedical applications.

articles.title_original: Advancing graphene-enabled piezoelectric, triboelectric, and hybrid nanogenerators: A review on mechanistic and performance optimization

articles.excerpt_original: Graphene significantly enhances the performance of piezoelectric (PENG), triboelectric (TENG), and hybrid piezoelectric-triboelectric (H-P/TENG) nanogenerators by regulating polarization, dielectric behavior, charge transport, and interfacial coupling. This review presents a critical analysis of graphene-enabled energy conversion through a unified Structure-Property-Mechanism-Performance (SPMP) framework, demonstrating how graphene governs the complete pathway from charge generation to practical power delivery. Unlike conventional reviews that emphasize voltage enhancement or material development in isolation, this work regards graphene's contribution to current-density optimization, charge synchronization, impedance matching, and energy-transfer efficiency as essential design principles in the transition from mechanical energy harvesting to the delivery of useable power and its subsequent integration with electrochemical energy-storage systems. The paper also critically examines the challenges that remain and highlights future research opportunities, focusing on scalable fabrication, long-term durability, power-management strategies, and the integration of harvesting with storage in order to achieve reliable self-powered wearable and Internet-of-Things systems.

articles.title_original: Tailoring the thermal conductivity of boron nitride-based materials through microstructural and architectural design for thermal management applications
articles.title_en: Review Maps Microstructural Strategies for Boron Nitride Thermal Management
articles.excerpt_original: The escalating power density of modern electronics has intensified the demand for thermal interface materials (TIMs) that simultaneously deliver high thermal conductivity and reliable electrical insulation. Hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) has emerged as a leading filler candidate; however, its practical performance remains constrained by interfacial phonon scattering and insufficiently interconnected conduction pathways. This review adopts a multi-scale structure–heat-transport perspective, systematically correlating BN microstructure, mesoscale orientation control via force, magnetic, and electric fields as well as freeze-casting, and three-dimensional thermal network construction with macroscopic thermal and mechanical performance. The discussion critically examines the extent to which interfacial bonding can be quantitatively correlated with interfacial thermal resistance (ITR), how vertical alignment can be reconciled with increasing filler loading, and whether oriented architectures can be scaled up without compromising structural integrity. This long-standing yet unresolved issues are shown to underlie the persistent gap between laboratory-scale thermal conductivity and device-level heat dissipation. Applications in the cooling of state-of-the-art electronic devices are highlighted, positioning BN-based materials as indispensable for next-generation thermal management.
articles.summary_en: A review examines how boron nitride microstructure, filler orientation, and three-dimensional thermal networks can improve thermal conductivity while preserving electrical insulation and mechanical integrity. It highlights interfacial thermal resistance and scale-up of oriented architectures as persistent barriers to device-level heat dissipation.

articles.title_original: Magnetically Reconfigurable Noncollinear Excitonic Polarization in a MoSe 2 /CrOCl/Fe 3 GaTe 2 Heterostructure
articles.title_en: Magnetically Reconfigurable Exciton Polarization Demonstrated in 2D Heterostructure
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Van der Waals (vdW) heterointerfaces provide a versatile platform for tailoring polarization‐resolved excitonic emission in 2D semiconductors, offering new opportunities for polarization‐encoded photonic functionalities. However, the realization of distinct and externally reconfigurable polarization orientations for coexisting excitonic states within a single magnetic heterostructure remains largely unexplored. Here we demonstrate magnetically reconfigurable exciton polarization in a MoSe 2 /CrOCl/Fe 3 GaTe 2 vdW heterostructure, arising from the combined effects of interfacial symmetry breaking and magnetically mediated interfacial coupling. Polarization‐resolved photoluminescence measurements reveal pronounced in‐plane anisotropy for both neutral excitons (X 0 ) and trions (T), with strongly non‐collinear polarization axes. Near the spin‐flop transition of CrOCl, the emission polarization undergoes an abrupt ∼ 90°rotation under an applied magnetic field, generating bistable polarization states that allow optical readout of magnetic phase evolution and dual‐channel polarization encoding. A further reorientation across the Néel temperature highlights the intimate coupling between magnetic order and lattice symmetry at the heterointerface. First‐principles calculations attribute the emergent anisotropy to anisotropic charge redistribution in MoSe 2 . These findings establish magnetic vdW heterointerfaces as a route to reconfigurable multi‐exciton polarization control and magnetic‐field‐tunable polarization encoding in 2D materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated bistable, magnetic-field-controlled polarization states in a MoSe₂/CrOCl/Fe₃GaTe₂ van der Waals heterostructure. The platform enables optical readout of magnetic phase changes and dual-channel polarization encoding for potential photonic and semiconductor applications.

articles.title_original: Design and functional testing of graphene/CNT TPU flexible piezoresistive sensor with nipple microstructure
articles.title_en: Graphene/CNT-TPU sensor enables seat-occupancy and sedentary alerts
articles.excerpt_original: Sedentary monitoring requires both tracking accumulated sitting time and confirming continuous seat occupancy. To overcome the limitation of software-based timing in directly sensing sitting pressure, this study presents a flexible piezoresistive sensor with a nipple microstructure, fabricated from graphene/CNT-TPU and embedded in a seat cushion to build a state-triggered sedentary reminder system. The device comprises a nipple-patterned TPU elastic substrate, a spray-coated graphene/CNT conductive layer, and a TPU encapsulation layer. Under pressure, recoverable deformation of the nipple structure and contact reconstruction of the carbon-based conductive network jointly modulate resistance. The pressure response shows segmented nonlinearity with slopes of 3.02, 1.35, and 0.58% kPa −1 . Stable response plateaus were obtained under stepwise loading at 5–100 kPa. Response and recovery times are about 180 and 260 ms, with stable periodic response after 7000 cycles. The sensor also distinguishes toe movements, mouse clicks, elbow and finger bending, and empty/500 mL bottle loads. Integrated into a seat cushion, it recorded continuous seat pressure from three subjects (45, 50, and 55 kg). The control system triggered an audible alert after 50 min of continuous pressure and ceased upon seat departure. These results demonstrate closed-loop integration of pressure sensing, occupancy detection, and sedentary alerting, providing a feasible flexible sensing solution for non-wearable seat occupancy monitoring.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a nipple-microstructured flexible piezoresistive sensor using graphene/CNT-TPU for continuous seat-pressure and occupancy monitoring. Integrated into a seat cushion, it delivered stable operation over 7,000 cycles and triggered an audible alert after 50 minutes of uninterrupted sitting.

articles.title_original: Phase-change metastructure with giant and tunable beam shifts for high-sensitivity mid-infrared sensing
articles.title_en: VO₂–hBN Metastructure Enables Tunable Mid-Infrared Sensing
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract We theoretically investigate a phase-change hyperbolic metastructure based on a VO 2 /hBN/VO 2 trilayer that enables actively tunable reflection-induced Goos-Hänchen (GH) and Imbert-Fedorov (IF) shifts in the mid-infrared regime under Gaussian beam. By synergistically integrating the reversible insulator-to-metal transition of vanadium dioxide (VO 2 ) with the anisotropic phonon-polaritons of hexagonal boron nitride (hBN), the proposed structure supports strong field confinement and sharp phase dispersion. Systematic analysis reveals that the trilayer configuration forms a Fabry-Pérot-like cavity, where dual-interface coupling and multiple reflections within the hBN spacer produce a reflection-phase gradient nearly an order of magnitude steeper than that of bilayer counterparts, directly accounting for the significant enhancement of both GH and IF shifts. Exploiting the sharp reflection-phase dispersion supported by the trilayer resonance, the metastructure is further extended to refractive-index sensing in both gaseous and biological environments. For NH 3 sensing, the GH-shift sensitivity reaches the order of 10 7 λ 0 /RIU. For biosensing, a sensitivity of 1.487×10 5 λ 0 /RIU is achieved for cancer cell detection. The results highlight the potential of VO 2 /hBN/VO 2 metastructures for high-performance, tunable infrared sensing and reconfigurable photonic devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers theoretically designed a VO₂/hBN/VO₂ phase-change metastructure that produces strongly enhanced, tunable beam shifts in the mid-infrared. articles.title_original: Epoxy Composites With Improved Thermal Conductivity and Low Viscosity for Electronic Packaging via Nanodiamond‐Decorated Boron Nitride Nanosheets
articles.title_en: Nanodiamond-Decorated Boron Nitride Improves Epoxy Thermal Conductivity
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Electronic packaging underfill materials require high thermal conductivity (TC) and low viscosity, but combining these in epoxy (EP) remains a critical bottleneck. Prefabricated skeleton networks or high filler content enhance EP's TC yet severely compromise viscosity. Therefore, improving TC at a relatively low filler content without significantly sacrificing viscosity is highly desirable. Here, a dense, uniform layer of nanodiamonds (ND) is decorated on the boron nitride nanosheets (BNNS) surface to fabricate BNNS@ND, which is then incorporated into EP to develop a BNNS@ND/EP composite. The anchored ND is proposed to suppress BNNS stacking, thereby favoring uniform dispersion of BNNS@ND and the formation of continuous heat‐conducting pathways at relatively low filler content in EP. The ND coating is also considered to improve interfacial compatibility between BNNS and EP, as well as to alleviate the viscosity increase of EP composite associated with BNNS stacking. Consequently, compared to pure EP, incorporating merely 30 phr BNNS@ND increases the TC by 522.2% to 1.12 W/(m·K) and raises the glass transition temperature ( T g ) by 25.1% to 133.8°C of BNNS@ND/EP, while the composite retains a low viscosity of 16.7 Pa·s. This work offers a feasible approach for electronic‐packaging polymer composites with exceptional TC, T g , and viscosity.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed an epoxy composite using nanodiamond-decorated boron nitride nanosheets to create conductive heat pathways at relatively low filler loading. The material increased thermal conductivity by 522.2% to 1.12 W/(m·K), while retaining low viscosity and improving glass-transition temperature, supporting electronic-packaging applications.

articles.title_original: Influence of synthesis temperature, amine concentration, and deposition voltage on the structural and dielectric properties of hBN/waterborne epoxy composite coatings
articles.title_en: Optimizing hBN–Epoxy Composite Coatings for Thermal and Dielectric Performance
articles.excerpt_original: Cationic waterborne epoxy composite coatings filled with hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) are increasingly vital in advanced semiconductor packaging and electronic power transistor heatsinks to provide electrical isolation while eliminating localized hot spots. However, electrophoretic deposition (EPD) lines suffer from various macroscopic defects—such as edge tearing and micro-voiding—due to poorly controlled pre-EPD resin amination parameters and turbulent high-voltage particle transport. This study implements a comprehensive three-factor Full Factorial design (27 runs) to map the independent and interactive influences of synthesis temperature (70 °C–130 °C), amination agent concentration (1.91–5.71 mL/L N -methylethanolamine), and EPD voltage (10–30 V) on composite coating properties. Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) demonstrates that amine concentration is the most dominant independent variable governing central coating thickness ( P = 0.002) and dielectric constant ( P = 0.014), while EPD voltage is statistically insignificant for central film thickness ( P = 0.851). High EPD voltages (30 V) trigger severe fringing field effects, resulting in structurally unviable edge configurations prone to tearing. To ensure optimal material processability, maximum structural uniformity, and stable dielectric property, a strict processing directive of 10 V EPD voltage coupled with a baseline resin amination matrix synthesized at 130 °C with 5.71 mL/L of amination agent is recommended.
articles.summary_en: A full-factorial study identified amine concentration as the strongest factor affecting coating thickness and dielectric constant in electrophoretically deposited hBN/waterborne epoxy composites. The researchers recommend 10 V deposition, with resin synthesized at 130 °C using 5.71 mL/L amination agent, to improve uniformity and prevent edge tearing.

articles.title_original: High-Fidelity Electrochemistry with Ultraclean Graphene Electrodes
articles.title_en: Ultraclean CVD Graphene Enables High-Fidelity Electrochemical Sensors
articles.excerpt_original: The electrochemical performance of CVD graphene electrodes has remained inconsistent and often inferior to that of exfoliated graphene, limiting their utility in analytical applications. This variability is widely attributed to structural disorder, but the dominant source remains unclear. Here, we show that amorphous carbon contamination introduced during synthesis is the primary factor governing the electrochemical behavior of CVD graphene. By eliminating this disorder during growth through oxygen-free CVD (OF-CVD), we obtain graphene electrodes that exhibit intrinsic and highly reproducible electrochemical behavior. Compared with conventional and commercial graphene, these electrodes display substantially enhanced heterogeneous electron-transfer kinetics, reduced charge-transfer resistance, and improved detection limits across both outer- and inner-sphere redox systems. Notably, they exhibit consistent anodic peak potentials across wide concentration ranges, nearly eliminating the concentration-dependent potential shifts characteristic of both glassy carbon and commercial/contaminated graphene electrodes. Further, microelectrode array architectures fabricated from this material suppress non-Faradaic background currents and exhibit steady-state diffusion behavior consistent with electrochemical theory, with improved signal-to-noise ratios. Together, these results establish that extrinsic carbon disorder has limited the electrochemical performance of CVD graphene to date. The removal of amorphous carbon reveals defect-free graphene's intrinsic electrochemical behavior and enables a reproducible, high-performance electrode platform, providing a clear pathway for reliable graphene-based electrochemical systems.
articles.summary_en: Researchers identify amorphous carbon contamination from synthesis—not structural disorder—as the primary cause of inconsistent CVD graphene electrochemistry. Oxygen-free CVD graphene electrodes show improved electron-transfer kinetics, lower resistance, detection limits, and signal-to-noise performance, supporting reproducible analytical sensor platforms.

articles.title_original: Use of Ultralow Dosages of Graphene to Enhance the Microstructural and Mechanical Properties of 3D-Printed Cementitious Mortars
articles.title_en: Ultralow graphene doses improve 3D-printed concrete performance
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Three-dimensional (3D) concrete printing offers an economical and sustainable option for rapid, formwork-free construction of geometrically unique structures. However, 3D-printed concrete elements often suffer from print-induced anisotropy and reduced mechanical performance. This study investigates the use of two novel graphene derivatives—fractal graphene (FG) and reactive graphene (RG)—as multifunctional nano-modifiers to overcome the aforementioned limitations associated with 3D-printed concrete. The influence of ultralow dosages (0.02% by mass of binder) of FG and RG on early-age heat release in graphene-modified pastes and the porosity and direction-dependent mechanical properties of 3D-printed elements are reported. FG and RG accelerate early hydration kinetics, with RG inducing a more pronounced shift in the acceleration peak due to its functionalized surfaces. Significant reductions in total porosity and critical pore diameter are noticed. Enhancements of up to 25% in compressive and flexural strengths are observed. The anisotropy in compressive strength is shown to be reduced by up to 50% through the use of FG or RG, indicating improved structural homogeneity. The graphene-modified specimens also exhibit enhanced strain capacity and improved crack-bridging behavior. These findings demonstrate the ability of ultralow dosages of FG and RG to simultaneously enhance hydration, refine microstructure, and improve mechanical properties of 3D-printed cementitious materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers found that 0.02% graphene derivatives reduced porosity and compressive-strength anisotropy in 3D-printed cementitious mortars. The additives also increased compressive and flexural strength by up to 25%, while improving hydration, strain capacity, and crack bridging.

articles.title_original: Bifunctional MXene-Pd multilayer electrodes enabling coupled electrochemical reforming and hydrogen evolution
articles.title_en: MXene–Pd multilayer electrodes improve electrochemical hydrogen production
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Conventional water splitting requires high overpotentials, whereas electrochemical reforming offers a sustainable route to produce hydrogen while oxidizing alcohols. In this work, we report the rational design of structurally ordered multilayer thin-film electrodes via electrostatic layer-by-layer (LbL) assembly, employing palladium nanoparticles (Pd NPs) as active electrocatalytic sites for both methanol oxidation reaction (MOR) and hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), and MXene as a multifunctional conductive support. The sequential assembly of negatively charged MXene nanosheets and positively charged Pd NPs produced well-defined (MXene/Pd) multilayers, which delivered a high MOR current density of 9.38 mA cm − 2 . This performance significantly surpasses that of other Pd-based multilayer electrodes, primarily due to the role of MXene in preventing NPs agglomeration, providing superior electrical conductivity, and, in the case of HER, contributing its own intrinsic hydrogen adsorption-desorption activity, which synergistically enhances the overall catalytic performance together with Pd. Furthermore, in two-electrode full-cell configurations, peak voltages of 0.9 V with a Pt cathode and 0.65 V with a (MXene/Pd) cathode were achieved, both below the theoretical water-splitting voltage of 1.23 V. The cooperative integration of Pd and MXene thus maximizes both methanol oxidation and hydrogen evolution, presenting a viable alternative to Pt-based catalysts. This study highlights the potential of LbL-engineered hybrid electrodes as a scalable and high-performance platform for electrochemical reforming and clean energy applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed layer-by-layer MXene–palladium multilayer electrodes that combine methanol oxidation with hydrogen evolution. The electrodes achieved 9.38 mA cm⁻² methanol-oxidation current density and operated below the theoretical water-splitting voltage, indicating potential for lower-energy hydrogen production.

articles.title_original: Interface-engineered hexagonal boron nitride modified PANI/MWCNTs nanocomposites for flexible symmetric supercapacitor in functionalized PVA/H2SO4 gel electrolyte
articles.title_en: h-BN/rGO Nanocomposite Enables Flexible Solid-State Supercapacitors
articles.excerpt_original: Developing energy storage devices that combine excellent electrochemical performance with mechanical compliance is critical for wearable and flexible electronics and cannot be achieved with traditional current collectors or leakage-prone liquid electrolytes. Herein, we describe a flexible all-solid-state supercapacitor based on a ternary nanocomposite electrode comprising polyaniline (PANI), multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs), and hexagonal boron nitride nanosheets (h-BNNs). The current collector is made of copper foil coated with reduced graphene oxide (rGO), which enhances its Young's modulus and corrosion resistance under acidic conditions. In the composite, h-BNNs act as structural and thermal buffers that hinder MWCNTs restacking and dissipate Joule heat, protecting PANI from pulverization during redox cycling; MWCNTs form a percolating conductive network, and PANI provides pseudocapacitive charge storage. The developed electrodes are symmetrically paired with an h-BNN-functionalized poly (vinyl alcohol)/H 2 SO 4 gel electrolyte, in which the h-BNN filler facilitates Grotthuss-type proton hopping and overcomes the sluggish ion diffusion observed in solid-state electrolytes. The hierarchical, interconnected porous architecture delivers a high specific capacitance of 289 F/g at 5 mV/s, together with an energy density of 32.4 Wh/kg and a power density of 449.7 W/kg, while maintaining 91% capacitance retention after 5000 cycles. This synergistic composite design, comprising a mechanically reinforced current collector, a thermally stabilized pseudocapacitive composite, and a fast-ion-conducting gel electrolyte, provides a generalizable strategy to bridge the performance gap between liquid- and solid-state supercapacitors, thereby enabling flexible energy storage for
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a flexible all-solid-state supercapacitor using PANI/MWCNT/h-BN electrodes, an rGO-coated copper current collector, and an h-BN-functionalized PVA/H2SO4 gel electrolyte. The device achieved 289 F/g specific capacitance, 32.4 Wh/kg energy density, and 91% capacitance retention after 5,000 cycles, indicating potential for wearable energy storage.

articles.title_original: Unveiling Carrier‐Mediated Acoustic Leakage as a Hidden Loss Pathway in Piezoelectric‐Semiconductor Heterostructures
articles.title_en: Carrier-Mediated Acoustic Leakage Identified in Piezoelectric Semiconductor Devices
articles.excerpt_original: Heterogeneous integration of dissimilar functional materials enables advanced micro/nano devices with unprecedented functionalities, yet the resulting interfacial multiphysics interactions can introduce hidden energy leakage pathways beyond conventional bulk systems. Here, we reveal a previously overlooked carrier-mediated acoustic leakage mechanism in piezoelectric-semiconductor heterostructures. By developing an electromechanical-carrier coupling model, we demonstrate that interfacial carrier accumulation reconstructs electrical boundary conditions, causing piezoelectric fields to penetrate into non-resonant regions. The resulting electric field distortion activates parasitic mechanical vibrations, which radiate bulk acoustic waves into the silicon substrate and degrade the quality (Q) factor. Ultrafast femtosecond laser pump-probe spectroscopy is further employed to characterize carrier dynamics, establishing a quantitative link between carrier modulation and acoustic performance. Guided by this mechanism, multiphysics decoupling strategies based on material engineering and electric field engineering are developed to suppress carrier-mediated acoustic leakage. By reconstructing electrical boundaries through defect-state modulation and asymmetric electrode design, the Q factor of piezoelectric-semiconductor devices is substantially enhanced while maintaining compatibility with standard fabrication processes. This work reveals an unconventional role of semiconductor carriers as mediators of acoustic energy redistribution and provides a mechanism-guided strategy for designing high-performance heterogeneously integrated micro/nano devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers identify a carrier-mediated acoustic leakage mechanism in piezoelectric–semiconductor heterostructures that degrades device quality factors. Material and electric-field engineering strategies, including defect-state modulation and asymmetric electrodes, are proposed to suppress leakage while retaining standard fabrication compatibility.

articles.title_original: Impact dynamic buckling of graphene platelets reinforced functionally graded rods
articles.title_en: Graphene-Platelet Composites Show Time-Dependent Impact Buckling
articles.excerpt_original: The dynamic buckling behaviours of functionally graded (FG) rods reinforced with graphene platelets (GPLs) under axial impact are comprehensively analysed using the energy method, with particular emphasis on explicitly accounting for the effects of stress wave propagation. The effective material properties are determined using modified Halpin-Tsai and Voigt-Reuss models for three distributions of GPLs through the thickness. Accounting for stress wave effects, a Lagrange function is formulated with trial functions satisfying boundary conditions. A time-dependent governing equation is derived and solved for three constraint types to obtain the critical buckling velocities. Numerical results examine how distribution patterns, geometry, GPL content, impact mass, and boundary conditions affect the critical velocities. The main findings highlight that impact-induced buckling is not instantaneous but rather a time-dependent process that varies significantly across different GPL distributions, providing crucial insights for the impact-resistant design of FG composite structures.
articles.summary_en: A study models dynamic buckling in functionally graded rods reinforced with graphene platelets, incorporating stress-wave propagation under axial impact. Results show that critical buckling velocity depends on platelet distribution, geometry, concentration, impact mass, and boundary conditions, informing impact-resistant composite design.

articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Extreme-intensity KrF excimer laser systems operating at 248 nm represent one of the most promising driver technologies for next-generation inertial confinement fusion due to their high wall-plug efficiency, short wavelength, and favorable laser-plasma coupling characteristics. However, achieving ignition-level implosion symmetry requires exceptionally high temporal pulse contrast, since amplified spontaneous emission (ASE) and prepulse components may initiate premature target ablation before the arrival of the main compression pulse. This work proposes an Adaptive Plasma Mirror (APM) architecture based on a low-Z regenerative Li₂BNH₆ composite medium reinforced with trace graphene concentrations and stabilized using 1–2 wt.% hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN). articles.title_original: Impact of optical nonlocality on the dispersion and propagation properties of in-plane exciton polaritons in monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides
articles.title_en: Optical Nonlocality Reshapes Exciton-Polariton Propagation in WS₂
articles.excerpt_original: In-plane exciton polaritons (IEPs) in monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides offer extreme electromagnetic field confinement and reduced losses for next-generation nanophotonics. To address this fundamental challenge, we present a rigorous theoretical framework incorporating spatial dispersion to evaluate IEPs in a hexagonal boron nitride (hBN)-encapsulated WS2 heterostructure. We calculate the microscopic exciton behavior by solving the Mott–Wannier equation with a statically screened Coulomb interaction evaluated using the quantum electrostatic heterostructure model. Utilizing these wavefunctions within linear response theory, we derive a nonlocal electric susceptibility tensor, which is then integrated into a transfer matrix method to simulate the macroscopic electrodynamic response. Our results demonstrate that nonlocality alters IEP dispersion relations by suppressing the unphysical high-momentum states predicted by local models, thereby shifting polariton modes toward lower wavevectors. This suppression mitigates extreme spatial damping, slightly weakening confinement while facilitating the long-range propagation of polariton modes. Furthermore, we reveal that the simultaneous excitation of the fundamental 1s and higher-order 2s excitonic states leads to spatial interference, and their relative energy transfer ratio can be modulated by varying the hBN encapsulation thickness. articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a theoretical framework incorporating spatial dispersion to model in-plane exciton polaritons in hBN-encapsulated monolayer WS₂. The results indicate that nonlocality suppresses unphysical high-momentum states, slightly reduces confinement, and enables longer-range polariton propagation for nanophotonic device design.

articles.title_original: Highly Sensitive Broadband Photodetectors Based on Donor–Acceptor 2D Conjugated Coordination Polymers
articles.title_en: Ni-TABQ 2D Coordination Polymer Enables Broadband Photodetection
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Two‐dimensional (2D) semiconductors are highly desirable for broadband photodetection but are often constrained by their limited optical absorption and inefficient exciton dissociation. In this study, we report a donor–acceptor‐engineered 2D conjugated coordination polymer (c‐CP), Ni‐TABQ (TABQ = tetraaminobenzoquinone), as a narrow‐bandgap semiconductor. The TABQ ligands integrate electron‐rich amino donors and electron‐deficient quinone carbonyl acceptors within the same molecular backbone, endowing the Ni‐TABQ lattice with strong intramolecular charge‐transfer absorption and a built‐in driving force for charge separation. Benefiting from strong broadband absorption and high charge‐carrier mobility, the vapor‐phase‐grown Ni‐TABQ thin films enable photodetection from 350 to 1400 nm under a 3 V bias, with a measurable response tail above 1150 nm, further achieving a responsivity of up to 3.1 A W −1 , a specific detectivity of up to 6.58 × 10 10 Jones (625 nm at ∼85 µW cm −2 ), and a response time of ∼206 µs, while maintaining stable operation at 3 V over 8500 s of continuous cycling. These metrics compare favorably with state‐of‐the‐art broadband photodetectors based on standalone 2D materials, establishing donor–acceptor molecular engineering within the 2D metal‐organic lattice as an effective strategy for advancing high‐performance 2D optoelectronic devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed vapor-phase-grown Ni-TABQ thin films, a narrow-bandgap 2D conjugated coordination polymer with photodetection spanning 350–1400 nm. The devices achieved responsivity up to 3.1 A W⁻¹, detectivity of 6.58 × 10¹⁰ Jones, and approximately 206 μs response times, indicating potential for high-performance broadband optoelectronics.

articles.title_original: A cross-layer 2D photodetection framework for standardized readout and signal fusion
articles.title_en: Cross-layer framework improves 2D photodetector signal processing
articles.excerpt_original: Beyond improving device responsivity, a central challenge in photodetectors based on two-dimensional (2D) materials is to resolve the information-interface mismatch and delayed system translation caused by trap-governed persistent photoconductivity (PPC). Here we present a cross-layer engineering route oriented towards practical implementation that integrates defect-mechanism analysis, non-stationary signal definition, dynamic distortion compensation and readout-interface engineering, thereby establishing a conversion pathway from physical response to system output in 2D MoS2, WSe2 and PtSe2 photodetectors. In this context, drift, hysteresis and fatigue accumulation in time-varying photoresponses are no longer treated merely as non-ideal perturbations, but are reformulated as state-dependent information that can be defined, compensated and interfaced. Through interface restructuring and stable readout, nW-level state-dependent photocurrents are systematically mapped onto a mixed-signal readout interface. We further extend this strategy to array-level unified output and multisensor fusion, with its frequency-guided representation evaluated in a machine-vision task. articles.summary_en: Researchers present an engineering framework for compensating persistent photoconductivity, drift, hysteresis and fatigue in MoS2, WSe2 and PtSe2 photodetectors. The approach standardizes readout across arrays and supports multisensor fusion for machine-vision applications, advancing 2D photodetectors toward system-level deployment.

articles.title_original: Quasi‐2D perovskite memristors: From layered structures to advanced computing applications
articles.title_en: Review links quasi-2D perovskite structure to more reliable memristors
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Metal halide perovskites are promising active materials for memristive devices, as their soft ionic lattices and mixed ionic–electronic conduction enable resistance switching under external bias. In conventional bulk 3D perovskites, however, uncontrolled ion migration and poor environmental stability undermine switching reliability. Quasi‐2D layered perovskites provide additional structural degrees of freedom to mitigate these limitations through a multiple‐quantum‐well architecture, where hydrophobic organic interlayers can suppress leakage currents and spatially constrain ionic transport. Although quasi‐2D perovskites have been increasingly studied for memristive applications, most reviews discuss them within the broader context of halide perovskites, often extending mechanisms from 3D systems without adequately accounting for the distinct ionic and electronic transport pathways introduced by the layered structure. This review provides a systematic framework linking the layered structure of quasi‐2D perovskites, including phase type, layer thickness, spacer‐cation chemistry, and film orientation, to their resistive switching behavior and device performance. The major switching mechanisms are examined, and the roles of dimensional and interfacial engineering in enhancing reliability, energy efficiency, and analog conductance modulation are comprehensively assessed. Rather than treating ion migration solely as a drawback, this review highlights how controlled ionic motion in quasi‐2D perovskites can be harnessed for stable memristive functionality. Emerging applications in neuromorphic computing, optoelectronic sensing, and in‐memory architectures are discussed, together with key challenges that must be addressed for practical deployment.
articles.summary_en: A review examines how layered quasi-2D perovskite architecture, spacer chemistry, thickness, and film orientation influence resistive switching. It highlights controlled ion migration for energy-efficient neuromorphic computing, optoelectronic sensing, and in-memory applications.

articles.title_original: Graphene Oxide Has Inhibitory Effects on Diverse Soil-Borne Pathogens
articles.title_en: Graphene Oxide Inhibits Diverse Soil-Borne Pathogens
articles.excerpt_original: Soil-borne diseases pose a major threat to global vegetable production, yet effective and environmentally friendly control strategies remain limited. In this study, the inhibitory effects of graphene oxide (GO) were systematically investigated against six soil-borne pathogens: three formae speciales of a single fungal species, Fusarium oxysporum (f. sp. niveum, cucumerinum and lycopersici), one bacterial pathogen (Pectobacterium carotovorum), one protist (Plasmodiophora brassicae) and one nematode (Meloidogyne incognita). In vitro assays demonstrated that GO exhibited concentration-dependent inhibition across all pathogens. At 200 mg·L−1, GO reduced mycelial biomass by 64–68%, spore germination by 38–44%, and colony diameter by 13–21% across three Fusarium formae speciales. GO also suppressed P. carotovorum colony-forming units by 65% and increased M. incognita mortality to 59.4%. Notably, GO showed exceptional efficacy against P. brassicae, reducing root hair infection by 86.2% and inhibiting dormant spore germination by 85.6%. In pot experiments, GO applied at 100 mg·kg−1 soil significantly reduced Fusarium wilt incidence and clubroot incidence by 59.8% and 57.3%, respectively. qPCR analysis confirmed that GO treatment reduced the abundance of target pathogens in soil. These results indicated that GO was a promising nanomaterial for the integrated management of soil-borne diseases.
articles.summary_en: An MDPI study found concentration-dependent graphene oxide inhibition of fungal, bacterial, protist and nematode pathogens in vitro. Soil applications also reduced Fusarium wilt and clubroot incidence, indicating potential for nanomaterial-based crop disease management.

At 4 and 8 weeks post_injection, disc tissues were harvested for histology and NPC counting. Histological analysis revealed restored annulus fibrosus integrity, even NPC distribution, reduced central cavity, and enhanced proteoglycan recovery. articles.summary_en: Researchers developed an injectable thermosensitive graphene oxide/polymer hydrogel that improved nucleus pulposus cell survival and proliferation in vitro. In a mouse disc-degeneration model, the hydrogel supported tissue repair and restored cell counts toward sham levels over eight weeks, indicating promising but preclinical potential.

articles.title_original: Enhanced and tunable light absorption in graphene hybrid quasi-BIC structures
articles.title_en: Graphene q-BIC Structures Enable Tunable Near-Infrared Absorption
articles.excerpt_original: This work investigates the integration of graphene into asymmetric Si/SiO₂ dielectric structures supporting quasi-bound states in the continuum (q-BICs) in the near-infrared range (1200–1600 nm). Numerical analysis of TE and TM modes shows that controlled symmetry breaking transforms ideal BICs into accessible q-BIC resonances, enabling efficient coupling with incident radiation. Optimized designs exhibit strongly enhanced absorption, reaching nearly 50%, due to intense electromagnetic confinement and high quality factors. Operating in a critical coupling regime, the hybrid structure balances radiative and graphene losses, achieving absorption far exceeding graphene’s intrinsic value. These results demonstrate the potential of q-BIC–graphene platforms for reconfigurable photonic modulators, high-sensitivity sensors, and adaptive near-infrared devices
articles.summary_en: Researchers integrated graphene into asymmetric silicon/silicon dioxide quasi-bound-state-in-continuum structures, achieving nearly 50% near-infrared absorption through enhanced electromagnetic confinement and critical coupling. The platform could support reconfigurable photonic modulators, high-sensitivity sensors, and adaptive infrared devices.

articles.title_original: Portable laser-induced graphene sensor for trace picric acid detection in water
articles.title_en: Portable Laser-Induced Graphene Sensor Detects Trace Picric Acid in Water
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract A portable electrochemical sensor based on laser-induced graphene (LIG) electrodes modified with graphene/PEDOT:PSS [Poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) polystyrene sulfonate] hybrid ink is developed for the trace-level detection of picric acid in water. The structural and compositional characterization of the LIG is performed using scanning electron microscopy, and energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy, confirming the successful formation of a conductive graphene network. The working electrode is further modified with graphene/PEDOT:PSS hybrid ink to enhance electrochemical performance. At neutral pH, the sensor exhibited two linear detection ranges of 25–500 nM and 1–25 µ M, with corresponding limits of detection of 50 nM and 3.8 µ M, respectively. Selectivity studies are conducted using common waterborne interfering species, including lead ions, ammonia, hydrazine, nitrate, and hydrogen peroxide, and the results demonstrated high selectivity toward picric acid within the potential window of −1.5 V to +0.2 V. The sensor showed good reproducibility across different devices ( n = 7) with deviations below 5%, and acceptable repeatability with deviations in the range of 6%–10%. Real sample analysis is performed using lake water spiked with picric acid, yielding recovery values exceeding 95%. Additionally, numerical optimization and experimental electrochemical impedance spectroscopy validation of the interdigitated electrode geometry are provided.
articles.summary_en: IOP Publishing researchers developed a portable electrochemical sensor using laser-induced graphene electrodes and a graphene/PEDOT:PSS hybrid ink for picric acid detection in water. The sensor achieved detection limits as low as 50 nM, showed strong selectivity and reproducibility, and recovered more than 95% of spiked picric acid from lake-water samples.

articles.title_original: Graphene-Like-Armored Nanosheet Assemblies toward Fast and Stable High-Mass-Loading Sodium Storage
articles.title_en: Graphene-Like Armor Enables High-Loading, Long-Life Sodium-Ion Anodes
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Sodium-ion batteries represent promising energy storage devices, yet their deployment is severely hampered by sluggish ion-transport kinetics and unstable electrode–electrolyte interfacial chemistry that deteriorate rate capability and cycling lifespan, particularly under high-loading electrode configurations. Here, we report a structural anode design comprising double-shelled TiO2 spheres assembled from cross-distributed 2 nm thick nanosheets and uniformly encapsulated by a graphene-like armor. This architecture enables predominantly surface-controlled sodium storage behavior with ultrafast reaction kinetics and exceptional stability, overcoming the long-standing trade-off between capacity, rate performance, and cycle life. The rationally designed electrode achieves a practically relevant areal capacity of 2.13 mAh cm–2 and outstanding rate capability (121 mAh g–1 at 100 C). Remarkably, it remains more than 90% of its capacity over 3,000 cycles at 5 C under a high mass loading of 10.5 mg cm–2, outperforming conventional anode structures. This work establishes a structural design strategy for advanced anodes applicable in practical high-power batteries.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed double-shelled TiO₂ nanosheet spheres encapsulated in a graphene-like layer for sodium-ion battery anodes. The design delivered 2.13 mAh cm⁻² areal capacity, 121 mAh g⁻¹ at 100 C, and over 90% capacity retention after 3,000 cycles at high mass loading.

articles.title_original: Interface-Programmed Growth of High-Aspect-Ratio 1D Ni–MOF Nanofibers on MXene for Wearable Enzyme-Free Glucose Sensing
articles.title_en: MXene–Ni-MOF Nanofibers Enable Wearable Enzyme-Free Glucose Sensors
articles.excerpt_original: Noninvasive wearable glucose sensors capable of real-time sweat analysis offer a less discomforting alternative for long-term monitoring in patients with diabetes. However, practical implementation remains challenging. Major barriers include insufficient catalytic sensitivity to quantify the low glucose levels in sweat, limited compatibility between nanomaterial synthesis and scalable manufacturing processes, and the lack of a biofluid microenvironment suitable for enzyme-free electrochemical sensing. Here, we address these challenges by combining strong interfacial anchoring on a conductive template with surfactant-assisted growth control to engineer high-aspect-ratio (∼100) 1D Ni-TCPP MOF nanofibers as an active shell on MXene-NH2. In contrast to conventional electrospinning-assisted approaches, the resulting 1D MOF shell is polymer-template-free and thus avoids insulating scaffold components. The resulting fluffy, self-supporting Ni-MOF@MXene architecture is inherently compatible with printed electronics, enabling large-area fabrication of wearable enzyme-free glucose-sensing patches. To overcome the constraints of enzyme-free sensing in physiological biofluids, we further develop an integrated system that combines microfluidics with a NaOH/Nafion/PVA alkaline sustained-release membrane, establishing a localized alkaline microenvironment within sweat to enable continuous analysis.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed high-aspect-ratio nickel–MOF nanofibers anchored on MXene for printed, wearable sweat-glucose sensing. Integrated microfluidics and a sustained-release alkaline membrane create a localized environment for continuous enzyme-free electrochemical analysis.

articles.title_original: Laser Writing of Hexagonal Boron Nitride Patterns with Low Global Thermal Budget
articles.title_en: Laser Writing Enables Low-Temperature Integration of Hexagonal Boron Nitride
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Direct integration of hexagonal boron nitride with temperature-sensitive substrates is constrained by the high global temperatures used in conventional growth. Here, we combine low-temperature deposition of an ammonia-borane-derived precursor on SiO2/Si (substrate temperature ≈ 70 °C) with spatially confined conversion by a focused 532-nm continuous-wave laser under ambient surroundings. Laser-written regions develop a persistent Raman band near 1370 cm–1 with a full width at half-maximum of 56.41 cm–1, and hyperspectral Raman imaging localizes this response to the irradiated sites. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy shows dominant B–N bonding and a B/N atomic ratio of 1.24 after conversion. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy reveals short, curved layered fringes with a median spacing of 0.349 nm, while scanning transmission electron microscopy–energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy establish nanocrystalline order and spatially colocated B and N within an oxygen-bearing, heterogeneous material. This approach enables low-temperature integration of hexagonal boron nitride with temperature-sensitive electronic and photonic platforms.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated localized conversion of an ammonia-borane-derived precursor into hexagonal boron nitride using a focused 532 nm laser after deposition at approximately 70 °C. The process could support integration of hBN with temperature-sensitive electronic and photonic platforms while limiting global thermal exposure.

articles.title_original: van der Waals Distributed Bragg Reflectors with Submicron Thickness for Enhanced WSe2 Photodetector Performance
articles.title_en: Van der Waals Reflectors Boost WSe2 Photodetector Responsivity 18.5-Fold
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Distributed Bragg reflectors (DBRs) are essential passive photonic components for spectral selectivity and optical field confinement, yet high-performance DBRs remain largely absent from the van der Waals (vdW) materials platform. Here we report a submicron-thick vdW DBR composed of alternating multilayer tungsten disulfide (WS2) and hexagonal boron nitride (hBN), establishing a compact passive optical building block for all-vdW photonics. Enabled by the large refractive-index contrast between multilayer WS2 and hBN, the 576 nm-thick DBR exhibits an experimental reflectance exceeding 97% and a stopband spanning 660 to 1060 nm. When integrated with tungsten diselenide (WSe2), the vdW DBR increases the layer-resolved absolute absorptance of the ∼4 nm WSe2 layer from 8% to 34% near the excitonic resonance, and photodetectors incorporating the DBR show an approximately 18.5-fold enhancement in responsivity at 750 nm relative to bare devices. Additional molybdenum disulfide (MoS2)/hBN DBR further demonstrates that the design is generalizable across transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD)/hBN material systems. These results show that layered vdW materials can serve not only as active optoelectronic media but also as high-performance passive photonic components, opening a route toward compact, integrable all-vdW optoelectronic and on-chip photonic platforms.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a submicron distributed Bragg reflector from alternating WS2 and hBN layers, achieving over 97% reflectance and enhancing WSe2 absorptance. Integrated photodetectors showed an approximately 18.5-fold responsivity increase at 750 nm, demonstrating a route to compact all-vdW photonic devices.

articles.title_original: Photothermal-Amplified Enzyme-Catalyzed Cascade Based on Gold Nanoparticle-Decorated MXene Overcoming H2O2 Barrier for Synergistic Tumor Therapy
articles.title_en: Gold-Decorated MXene Platform Enables Synergistic Photothermal Tumor Therapy
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract MXenes have emerged as promising two-dimensional nanomaterials for cancer nanomedicine owing to their tunable surface chemistry, strong photothermal response, and favorable biocompatibility. Herein, we develop a gold nanoparticles-decorated MXene nanoplatform (Au@Mo2TiC2Tx-PEG) for synergistic photothermal and catalytic tumor therapy. The nanoplatform is constructed by anchoring Au nanoparticles onto Mo2TiC2Tx nanosheets, followed by polyethylene glycol modification to improve physiological stability and biocompatibility. The as-prepared Au@Mo2TiC2Tx-PEG exhibits strong near-infrared absorption with a photothermal conversion efficiency of 39.8%, enabling effective photothermal therapy under 808 nm laser irradiation. Notably, this nanoplatform possesses intrinsic glucose oxidase (GOx)-like and peroxidase (POD)-like activities, which initiate a cascade catalytic reaction within the tumor microenvironment. Glucose oxidation-mediated H2O2 generation, which subsequently converts into highly cytotoxic reactive oxygen species, while simultaneously depleting intracellular glutathione disrupts tumor redox homeostasis. The integrated catalytic and photothermal effects synergistically enhance oxidative stress, promote tumor cell apoptosis, and improve therapeutic efficacy. Both in vitro and in vivo studies reveal that Au@Mo2TiC2Tx-PEG effectively suppresses tumor progression, achieving a tumor inhibition rate of 94% under 808 nm laser irradiation with minimal systemic toxicity. These findings demonstrate the potential of the MXene-based nanoplatform to integrate catalytic metabolism regulation and photothermal activation, providing a powerful strategy for precision cancer therapy.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a PEG-stabilized gold nanoparticle-decorated MXene platform that combines near-infrared photothermal therapy with glucose oxidase- and peroxidase-like catalytic activity. In vitro and in vivo testing reported 94% tumor inhibition under 808 nm irradiation with minimal systemic toxicity, supporting further investigation for precision cancer therapy.

articles.title_en: Graphite Layer Improves hBN Quantum-Emitter Stability for Cryptography
articles.excerpt_original: Single-photon emitters are crucial components for quantum communication technologies. Two-dimensional materials like hexagonal boron nitride are a promising candidate for these technologies but are limited by their photoinstabilities which present a distinct challenge in producing on-demand high single-photon purity samples. In this manuscript, we show that the insertion of a conducting van der Waals layer like graphite increases the photostability of the hBN emitter, leading to improved photonic properties.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report that inserting a conducting graphite van der Waals layer improves the photostability and photonic properties of hexagonal boron nitride single-photon emitters. The result could support more reliable quantum communication and cryptographic technologies.

articles.title_original: Realization of Reversible Regulation of Thermal Conductivity in 2D Materials through Engineered Acoustic Mismatch
articles.title_en: Engineered Acoustic Mismatch Enables Reversible Thermal Conductivity Control in Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract In modern electronic devices, active control of heat transport is essential for performance and reliability, yet most existing approaches to thermal conductivity modulation are irreversible and fixed after synthesis. Here, we propose a reversible thermal conductivity regulation strategy based on engineered junctions in two-dimensional (2D) materials. By locally coupling the central region of a 2D heat-conducting layer to a substrate, we create a junction that exhibits distinct out-of-plane acoustic phonon (ZA mode) properties relative to the surrounding uncoupled region, thereby introducing an engineered acoustic mismatch to dynamically regulate heat transport. Using homogeneous nonequilibrium molecular dynamics (HNEMD) and nonequilibrium molecular dynamics (NEMD) simulations with a graphene/hexagonal boron nitride (Gr/h-BN) junction as a model system, we show that tuning the interlayer coupling in the junction region can suppress the thermal conductivity of graphene by up to a factor of 49 at 100 K. At room temperature (300 K), the modulation ratio can still reach 6.5. This effectiveness of this architecture is not limited by the type of substrates and heat-conducting layer, demonstrating excellent versatility and robustness. The proposed architecture offers a promising route toward dynamic, reversible thermal management in 2D materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers propose a reversible method for dynamically regulating heat transport in two-dimensional materials by locally coupling graphene to a substrate, creating an engineered acoustic mismatch. Simulations of graphene/hexagonal boron nitride junctions predict up to 49-fold conductivity suppression at 100 K and 6.5-fold modulation at room temperature, supporting potential thermal-management applications.

articles.title_original: Low-resistance ohmic contacts: a strategy for ideal 2D semiconductor transistors
articles.title_en: Strategies for Low-Resistance Contacts in 2D Semiconductor Transistors
articles.excerpt_original: The rapid development of two-dimensional (2D) transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) field-effect transistors (FETs) highlights the critical need to reduce the contact resistance for the future of Moore’s law using 2D complementary metal-oxide semiconductors. Electrical metal contacts with 2D TMDs-based FETs remain a critical challenge because of their high contact resistance, which primarily results from the Schottky barrier, poor interface quality, and Fermi level pinning. In this study, we report a significant reduction in the contact resistance of 2D TMDs using several strategies including plasma knowledge based polymorphic engineering, controllable doping, band matching, phase engineering and insertion buffer layer.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report approaches to reduce contact resistance in transition metal dichalcogenide field-effect transistors, addressing Schottky barriers, interface quality, and Fermi-level pinning. The strategies include polymorphic engineering, controlled doping, band matching, phase engineering, and buffer layers.

articles.title_original: Planar Macromolecular Semiconductors Enable Fast Electron‐Ion Transport Kinetics for High‐Performance Zinc‐Organic Batteries
articles.title_en: Planar Macromolecular Semiconductors Boost Zinc-Organic Battery Performance
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Polymer cathodes featuring versatile designable redox‐active motifs and structural anti‐dissolution in aqueous electrolytes have attracted interest for advancing zinc‐organic batteries. However, their implementation is hindered by insulating electronic properties and sluggish ion transport, both arising from twisted molecule chains with poor structural planarity, which limits active‐site accessibility and capacity delivery. Here we design planar macromolecular semiconductors (PMSs) by fusing a four‐electron pyrene‐4,5,9,10‐tetraone acceptor and a two‐electron tetraminobenzoquinone donator into long‐range conjugated polymeric skeletons through intermolecular π – π interactions. The highly π ‐extended planarity endows PMSs with a semiconducting property (7.64 × 10 −7 S cm −1 ) that promotes efficient electron delocalization, and yields the highest ion diffusion coefficient (6.52 × 10 −7 cm 2 s −1 ) among reported organic cathodes. Leveraging synergistic fast electron‐ion transport kinetics, the long‐range stacking of molecular planes minimizes conformational disorder, enabling near‐complete utilization (98.4%) of redox‐active quinone−phenazine motifs with an ultralow activation energy (0.19 eV). Consequently, Zn||PMSs battery liberates high capacities (442/263 mAh g −1 at 0.2/100 A g −1 ), alongside a long lifespan (60,000 cycles). Besides, PMSs cathode enables a 348 mAh zinc pouch cell with a high mass loading (20 mg cm −2 ) to operate stably for 1000 cycles. This work provides a promising direction to design planar organic semiconductors for boosting electron‐ion migration kinetics toward better zinc batteries.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed planar macromolecular semiconductor cathodes that accelerate electron and ion transport in aqueous zinc-organic batteries. The cells delivered up to 442 mAh g−1, retained performance for 60,000 cycles, and supported a 348 mAh pouch cell operating for 1,000 cycles.

articles.title_original: Evaluating the Stability of 2D Compounds: Effects of Temperature, Mechanical Support and Vibrational Degrees of Freedom
articles.title_en: Study Shows Pd Substrates Stabilize 2D MgO Monolayers
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The thermodynamic stability of two-dimensional (2D) materials remains a critical bottleneck in their synthesis and practical application. While Density Functional Theory (DFT) has revolutionized the characterization of these systems, standard 0 K computational protocols often overlook the complex interplay between thermal fluctuations and structural constraints. In this work, we investigate the stability of 2D MgO monolayers, examining how temperature, structural flexibility and mechanical support from a Pd substrate influence the material’s energy landscape. Our findings show that the thermodynamic behavior depends strongly on the structural degrees of freedom accessible in the simulations. Adequately large simulation cells are required to capture long-wavelength vibrational modes that significantly lower the free energy through entropic contributions. We demonstrate that while freestanding monolayers become unstable at finite temperatures, mechanical coupling with a substrate provides a crucial stabilizing effect while modifying the electronic band gap and atomic mobility. These results provide a more accurate framework for predicting the behavior of 2D compounds under realistic experimental conditions and highlight the importance of including vibrational entropy and substrate effects in computational studies of two-dimensional materials.
articles.summary_en: Computational research finds that freestanding 2D MgO monolayers become unstable at finite temperatures, while mechanical coupling to a palladium substrate improves stability. The study highlights the importance of vibrational entropy, structural flexibility and substrate effects in predicting realistic 2D-material behavior.

articles.title_original: Observation of electrically generated polaron-polaritons in a monolayer MoSe 2 microcavity
articles.title_en: Electrically Generated Polaron-Polaritons Demonstrated in Monolayer MoSe₂
articles.excerpt_original: Quasiparticles arising from the interaction between mobile impurities and a quantum many-body environment-known as polarons-play a pivotal role in shaping the optical and electronic properties of low-dimensional systems. Here, we report the direct observation of electrically generated polaron-polaritons within a monolayer molybdenum diselenide microcavity. By embedding the monolayer in a planar optical cavity, we achieve strong coupling between exciton-polarons and cavity photons, creating an electrically driven light-emitting diode based on polaron-polaritons. The device exhibits an external quantum efficiency of ∼0.15%, representing a 10-fold enhancement over prior exciton-polariton devices based on monolayer tungsten disulfide. This demonstration establishes a versatile platform for inversionless laser technology and for polariton-based quantum optoelectronics while offering insights into radiative many-body physics in two-dimensional semiconductors.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated electrically generated polaron-polaritons in a monolayer molybdenum diselenide microcavity, producing a light-emitting diode with approximately 0.15% external quantum efficiency. The work advances polariton-based quantum optoelectronics and potential inversionless laser platforms.

articles.title_original: III-Nitride ferroelectrics for information storage and processing at low power and in extreme environments
articles.title_en: III-Nitride Ferroelectrics Enable Low-Power Memory and 2D FETs
articles.excerpt_original: in this talk, I will try to make the case of how novel III-nitride materials might present interesting avenues to overcome some of the above limitations being faced by both Silicon and Silicon Carbide (SiC) hardware. I will start by presenting our ongoing and recent work on integration of 2D chalcogenide semiconductors emerging wurtzite structure ferroelectric nitride materials1 namely aluminium scandium nitride (AlScN). articles.title_original: Modeling approaches to support discovery of quantum properties of materials with validation by graphene studies
articles.title_en: Quantum Subspace Methods Validated on Graphene Models
articles.excerpt_original: Quantum subspace diagonalization (QSD) is a near-term strategy for electronic-structure problems that avoids the deep, heavily optimized circuits of the variational quantum eigensolver by preparing a small basis, measuring a subspace Hamiltonian on hardware, and diagonalizing it classically. We benchmark two QSD variants, a seniority-based orthogonal method (Q-SENSE) and a non-orthogonal correlated-basis method (CVQE), on a minimal two-site Hubbard model whose parameters correspond to a graphene (symmetric) and a hexagonal boron nitride-like (sublattice-broken) sublattice motif. Because the model is exactly solvable, hardware results are graded against the true ground state and against a Hartree-Fock mean-field baseline, isolating the correlation energy each method recovers. On IBM Heron superconducting processors we find that the symmetric case recovers essentially all of the correlation energy with inexpensive readout-error mitigation, whereas the gapped case is limited by two-qubit gate error on the hopping terms. On a single device (ibm_kingston), readout mitigation alone recovers 75% of the hBN correlation energy; adding zero-noise extrapolation reduces the per-run error and raises the mean recovery to 98% ± 18% (n=5), though the run-to-run variance remains large relative to the mean.
articles.summary_en: Researchers benchmarked two quantum subspace diagonalization methods on graphene- and hBN-like Hubbard models using IBM Heron processors. Readout mitigation recovered nearly all graphene correlation energy, while combined mitigation achieved 98% ± 18% mean recovery for the hBN-like case despite substantial variance.

articles.title_original: TERS imaging of 2D semiconductors: old mysteries and new materials
articles.title_en: TERS reveals orientation-independent spectra and layer modes in 2D semiconductors
articles.excerpt_original: In this talk we’ll present two stories related to the tip enhanced Raman scattering (TERS) imaging of 2D semiconductors. First, we’ll demonstrate recent results of TERS imaging of 1-4-layer ReS2 exfoliated to template-stripped gold. Conventional far-field Raman spectra of ReS2 feature up to 18 peaks within the 0-500 cm-1 range, while the intensity of individual peaks strongly depends on the mutual orientation of the polarization vector in the laser focus and the crystalline axes within the ReS2 plane. We demonstrate that unlike the far-field response, the gap-mode TERS spectra of ReS2 on gold do not change as a result of the sample rotation in the XY plane. We also show that in addition to the regular vibrational modes we can also observe the layer breathing modes in multilayer ReS2 crystals. In the second part we'll discuss the possible reasons for an unprecedented preferential enhancement of the 995 cm-1 mode in TERS spectra of α-MoO3 and how the fact that this mode falls within the Type I reststrahlen band may affect the TERS response and open the possibilities for the IR-Raman crosstalk.
articles.summary_en: Research demonstrates gap-mode TERS imaging of few-layer ReS₂ on gold, showing spectra that are insensitive to in-plane sample rotation and revealing multilayer breathing modes. The study also examines preferential enhancement of an α-MoO₃ vibrational mode and its potential implications for infrared–Raman cross-talk.

articles.title_original: Tip-enhanced quantum sensing spectroscopy for bright and high-purity single-photon emitters
articles.title_en: Tip-Enhanced Spectroscopy Enables Dynamic Control of Single-Photon Emitters
articles.excerpt_original: Bright and controllable single-photon emitters are essential for quantum information technologies, yet deterministic nanoscale control remains challenging. In this talk, I present recent advances in tip-enhanced quantum sensing spectroscopy for manipulating single-photon emitters such as colloidal quantum dots and defect centers in hexagonal boron nitride at room temperature. By employing scanning probe–based plasmonic cavities with strong local field enhancement and nanoscale precision, we demonstrate active tuning of emission spectra, dipole orientation, and photon statistics. I will discuss electric-field-assisted strong coupling spectroscopy and tip-enhanced nano-optical trapping, enabling dynamic control from weak to strong coupling regimes. These results establish a versatile platform for real-time quantum sensing and reconfigurable solid-state photon sources.
