articles.title_original: Intrinsic Photoresponses of As-Exfoliated Few-Layer MoS2 Phototransistors
articles.title_en: Suspended MoS2 Phototransistors Reveal Fast, Low-Noise Intrinsic Photoresponse
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The photoresponse of two-dimensional MoS2 photodetectors is often dominated by extrinsic effects, such as photoinduced Schottky barrier modulation and interfacial trap-induced photogating, which obscure the intrinsic material properties. To investigate the channel-dominated photoresponse of as-exfoliated few-layer MoS2, we fabricate suspended-channel phototransistors with bismuth-based Ohmic contacts to suppress major extrinsic effects from contacts and substrate interfaces. Through a direct comparison with conventional substrate-supported devices also with Ohmic contacts, we demonstrate that the suspended devices exhibit a fast response (45/83 μs rise/fall time) and a low-noise photocurrent consistent with a photoinduced narrowing of local depletion regions associated with defect states, described by a depletion-region modulation model originally developed for polycrystalline photoconductors. In contrast, conventional devices show orders-of-magnitude higher responsivity but suffer from slow, trap-dominated dynamics and significantly elevated noise. Parameter extraction from the photocurrent fitting reveals a minority carrier recombination lifetime of ∼2.03 ns in the suspended channel. This work clarifies the intrinsic photoresponse mechanism of MoS2 and underscores the critical role of interface engineering in realizing high-speed, low-noise photodetectors based on two-dimensional semiconductors.
articles.summary_en: Researchers isolated the intrinsic photoresponse of few-layer MoS2 using suspended channels and bismuth-based Ohmic contacts, achieving 45/83 μs rise/fall times and low-noise operation. The findings highlight interface engineering as a route to higher-speed, lower-noise two-dimensional photodetectors, while conventional devices showed higher responsivity but trap-dominated dynamics.

articles.title_original: Comparative Mechanisms of Graphene Nanoplatelets and Graphene Oxide in Regulating Pore Structure and Drying Shrinkage of Cement Mortar
articles.title_en: Graphene Oxide Outperforms Nanoplatelets in Cement Mortar
articles.excerpt_original: This study comparatively investigates the reinforcement mechanisms of graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs) and graphene oxide (GO) in cement mortar at dosages of 0–0.1%, focusing on mechanical properties, drying shrinkage, fluidity, water absorption, and microstructural evolution characterized by SEM, XRD, and MIP. Both nanomaterials reduce fluidity, with GO exhibiting a less pronounced effect. The mechanical properties display unimodal dosage-dependent trends, with optimal flexural strength at 0.05% and optimal compressive strength at 0.03%; the corresponding 28 d enhancements reach 16.9% and 20.8% for GO, compared with 8.2% and 8.5% for GNP. Water absorption and drying shrinkage attain minima at 0.03% and 0.05%, respectively. GO consistently outperforms GNP, which is attributed to its superior pore refinement, reducing total porosity by 15.0% and large pores (>100 nm) by 51.3%, owing to its functional groups that promote dispersion and hydration nucleation. These results establish GO as a more effective nano-reinforcement for pore-structure engineering in cementitious composites.
articles.summary_en: A comparative study finds graphene oxide improves 28-day flexural and compressive strength more than graphene nanoplatelets while reducing porosity, water absorption, and drying shrinkage at optimized dosages. Functional groups are linked to better dispersion, hydration nucleation, and pore refinement in cement mortar.

articles.title_original: MXene-based composite hydrogel with synergistic crosslinking networks for multimodal wearable sensors
articles.title_en: MXene Hydrogel Enables Multimodal Wearable Sensing
articles.excerpt_original: Flexible wearable sensors with multimodal sensing capabilities are urgently needed for personalized health monitoring and human–machine interaction. However, integrating high stretchability, excellent conductivity, and multiple stimulus responsiveness into a single hydrogel remains challenging. Herein, we develop a multifunctional MXene-based composite hydrogel PABSM (PVA, acrylic acid, borax, sodium alginate, and MXene) via one-pot free radical polymerization, incorporating poly(vinyl alcohol), acrylic acid, sodium alginate, bacterial cellulose, borax, and MXene nanosheets. The hydrogel features a synergistic crosslinking network comprising dynamic borate ester bonds, covalent crosslinks, hydrogen bonding, and electrostatic interactions. The PABSM hydrogel exhibits outstanding mechanical properties, high conductivity (1.27 S/m), and multimodal sensing capabilities, including strain sensitivity (gauge factor up to 1.96 over 0–1400 % strain) and thermal sensitivity (negative temperature coefficient of − 4.72 %/°C, R 2 = 0.995 ). The sensor demonstrates rapid response/recovery times (170 ms for pressure, 11 s/8.6 s for temperature), excellent cycling stability over 1000 cycles, and reliable monitoring of human motions including finger bending, wrist movement, knee flexion, and vocalization, with good biocompatibility. These properties position the PABSM hydrogel as a promising platform for wearable health monitoring, soft robotics, and human–machine interfaces.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a stretchable MXene-based composite hydrogel with conductivity, strain and thermal sensitivity, and rapid response. The material monitored body movements and vocalization, supporting potential applications in health monitoring, soft robotics, and human–machine interfaces.

articles.title_original: Bond-Switching Reconstruction in Bare Ti3C2 MXene
articles.title_en: Study Reveals Bond-Switching Reconstruction in Ti3C2 MXene
articles.excerpt_original: MXene properties are typically tuned through composition, surface termination, and intercalation, while the metal-carbon framework topology is considered fixed. Here, we demonstrate that this framework can reconstruct. Unconstrained relaxations of biaxially strained bare Ti3C2 yield a dynamically stable polymorph, N, featuring a 15-atom primitive cell, six distinct Ti-C bond classes, and 2.55 Å Ti-Ti pairs. The coherent transformation pathway crosses an 8.47 eV barrier per cell but first reaches another reconstructed minimum, N', lying 1.08 eV below N, revealing a family of bond-switched networks. Phase N lies 7.58 eV per cell above the parent. Reverse barriers along the calculated pathway are 1.50 and 1.98 eV per cell for N and N', respectively. Reconstruction quenches the parent spin polarization, yielding a nonmagnetic metal with a nearly fourfold increase in Fermi-level density of states. Bader and electron-localization analyses suggest charge redistribution from C toward Ti associated with Ti-Ti pairing. In multilayers, reconstructed layers form interlayer Ti-C bonds. A 10% biaxial tension halves the phase-energy difference, and pressure reverses phase ordering near 85 GPa. These results establish bond-switching reconstruction as a mechanically controllable structural degree of freedom in MXenes.
articles.summary_en: Computational research shows that strained bare Ti3C2 MXene can undergo bond-switching reconstruction into metastable polymorphs with altered magnetism, electronic density of states, and interlayer bonding. The findings identify mechanical strain and pressure as potential controls over MXene structure and properties.

articles.title_original: Vacuum-Assisted Assembly of GO/MXene Lamellae for Enhanced PES Nanofiltration Performance
articles.title_en: Vacuum-Assembled GO/MXene Membranes Improve Dye Nanofiltration
articles.excerpt_original: Polyethersulfone (PES) membranes suffer from intrinsic hydrophobicity and severe fouling, limiting their applicability in dye-containing wastewater treatment. In this study, thin-film composite PES/GO/MXene nanofiltration (NF) membranes were fabricated through a vacuum-assisted nano-intercalation strategy that enables controlled assembly of GO and MXene nanosheets on PES substrates. Systematic tuning of the GO-to-MXene ratio revealed clear correlations between lamellar structure, surface chemistry and the resulting water permeability, dye rejection, and antifouling behavior. The optimized membrane (GO:MXene = 1:2) achieved a high pure water permeance of 50.1 L·m −2 ·h −1 ·bar −1 together with rejection rates of 97.3% for methylene blue and 93.8% for rhodamine B. Moreover, the membrane demonstrated stable dye rejection and a flux recovery ratio of ∼84% over five bovine serum albumin fouling-cleaning cycles, demonstrating good short-term operational stability. This work provides a promising interfacial engineering strategy to incorporate mixed 2D lamellar nanochannels into polymeric NF membranes for efficient purification of dye-contaminated wastewater.
articles.summary_en: Researchers fabricated polyethersulfone membranes containing graphene oxide and MXene lamellae using vacuum-assisted nano-intercalation. The optimized membrane achieved 50.1 L·m⁻²·h⁻¹·bar⁻¹ water permeance, over 93% dye rejection, and approximately 84% flux recovery after fouling cycles.

articles.title_original: Fe-N-C matrix integrated with Selenium-modified-MXene to enhance oxygen reduction reaction
articles.title_en: Selenium-Modified MXene–Fe-N-C Catalyst Enhances Zinc–Air Battery Performance
articles.excerpt_original: Iron-nitrogen-carbon (Fe-N-C) materials have attracted considerable attention as promising noble-metal-free catalysts for the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR), yet their activity and durability remain limited. In this work, an integrated composite structure was rationally designed and constructed by Fe-N-C matrix integrated with Selenium-modified-MXene. This integrated architecture may facilitate electron transport, reactant accessibility, and intermediate conversion during ORR. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analyses indicate possible electronic interactions among Se species, Fe-N x coordination structures, and the MXene framework within the multiphase catalyst, which contribute to enhanced ORR kinetics. Meanwhile, the highly conductive MXene-derived component facilitate electron transport and interfacial charge transfer, improving the electrochemical reaction environment and interfacial stability. Benefiting from the synergistic interactions among Fe-N x coordination structures, Se-related species, and MXene interfaces, the resulting Se-MX@Fe-N-C catalyst exhibits good ORR activity, delivering a half-wave potential ( E 1/2 ) of 0.901 V, which is superior to commercial Pt/C (0.865 V), along with high power density (131.9 mW cm –2 ), large current density (257.3 mA cm –2 ), good Zn utilization capacity (761.8 mAh g Zn –1 ), and good cycling stability of up to 167 h when applied as the air cathode in Zinc-air batteries. This work offers insights into the rational design of multiphase Fe-N-C-based systems for efficient and durable energy conversion.
articles.summary_en: Researchers integrated selenium-modified MXene with an Fe-N-C catalyst, achieving an oxygen-reduction half-wave potential of 0.901 V, exceeding commercial Pt/C. The catalyst also delivered high power density and cycling stability in zinc–air batteries, supporting research into durable noble-metal-free air cathodes.

articles.title_original: Dynamic DNA logic circuits regulating CRISPR-Cas12a trans-cleavage on MXene for high-throughput miRNAs detection
articles.title_en: MXene-Based CRISPR Biosensor Enables Multiplexed miRNA Detection
articles.excerpt_original: For the early diagnosis of malignancies, microRNAs (miRNAs) serve as crucial biomarkers. However, the direct application of the CRISPR-Cas system for multiplexed miRNA screening is hindered by the "one-crRNA-to-one-target" limitation. To address this challenge, we report a programmable paper-based microfluidic biosensor integrating computer-aided designed dynamic DNA circuits with CRISPR-Cas12a system on MXene. Within this sensing architecture, specific dual-miRNA targets independently initiate catalytic hairpin assembly cascades, and two DNA activators are generated to form a strict "AND" logic gate. Afterwards, the simultaneous presence of both activators triggers the robust trans-cleavage activity of Cas12a, cutting fluorophore-labeled single stranded DNA probes on MXene and yielding effective fluorescence recovery. Herein, MXene serves as both substrate and superior quencher, dramatically suppressing background noise to guarantee high signal-to-background ratio. Thus, the combination of catalytic hairpin assembly and Cas12a achieves exponential signal amplification. Furthermore, a paper-based microfluidic device is constructed for high-throughput miRNAs detection in human serum. This work provides a novel strategy for precise miRNA detection in early molecular cancer diagnostics and point-of-care testing.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a paper-based microfluidic biosensor combining dynamic DNA logic circuits with CRISPR-Cas12a on MXene to detect dual miRNA targets using an AND-gate mechanism. The platform supports high-throughput detection in human serum and may enable early cancer diagnostics and point-of-care testing.

articles.title_original: Tiny Pores, Big Stories: Perforating MXenes for Through-Sheet Transport in Energy and Environmental Applications
articles.title_en: Perforated MXenes Enable Faster Through-Sheet Transport
articles.excerpt_original: Conspectus Transport remains a central bottleneck limiting the practical performance of MXene electrodes and membranes. Although MXenes possess metallic conductivity, hydrophilicity, and rich surface chemistry, their two-dimensional (2D) layered architecture imposes barriers to ion and molecular diffusion. During assembly into electrodes and membranes, colloidal MXene nanosheets readily restack and force transport mainly through thin interlayer galleries. The as-formed slit channels lengthen diffusion pathways leading to sluggish kinetics. These limitations become increasingly important in compact, high-loading MXene structures, where long and tortuous transport pathways can further reduce active-site utilization and rate capability. This Account argues that in-plane pore engineering transforms MXenes from predominantly lamellar-type materials into through-sheet transport platforms. Introducing nanopores into the MXene basal planes creates transverse pathways that directly connect neighboring interlayer galleries, thereby shortening diffusion distances and increasing edge-site and basal-plane accessibility. Holey MXenes therefore represent more than simply porous MXenes; they are transport-engineered 2D materials in which nanoscale perforation provides an additional direction for the movement of ions and molecules while retaining the intrinsic advantages of the MXene framework. This concept is particularly relevant to densely assembled electrodes and membranes, where in-plane pathways enable rapid mass transport. We summarize our efforts toward the synthesis and structural engineering of holey MXenes, including oxidative perforation of MXene hydrogels, microwave-assisted ultrafast etching, controlled H2O2-mediated perforation, and radical-intensified selective etching (
articles.summary_en: A review finds that nanopores in MXene nanosheets can create transverse pathways across layered electrodes and membranes, shortening ion and molecular diffusion distances. The approach may improve mass transport, active-site accessibility, and rate capability in compact energy and environmental applications.

articles.title_original: Thermal Interface Materials and Two-Dimensional Nanomaterials for High-Density Data Center Thermal Management
articles.title_en: Graphene-Based Thermal Interface Materials for High-Density Data Centers
articles.excerpt_original: The proliferation of high‑performance computing (HPC) and artificial intelligence (AI) workloads has given rise to unprecedented power densities in data center hardware, positioning thermal management as a critical bottleneck constraining system performance, long‑term reliability, and energy efficiency. This paper clarifies the role of advanced thermal interface materials (TIMs) in addressing thermal management challenges in high‑density data centers, with a particular focus on nanostructured systems and emerging two‑dimensional materials such as graphene and hexagonal boron nitride (h‑BN). Accordingly, this study analyzes the physical origins of thermal bottlenecks, including interfacial thermal resistance (ITR) and localized hotspots, and assesses the development and performance of advanced TIMs. And it further compares conventional particle‑filled composites with nanostructured materials, thus highlighting the interplay among material properties, interfacial heat transfer mechanisms, and practical implementation challenges. Results show that two‑dimensional nanomaterials provide promising solutions through enhanced thermal transport and interface engineering, although limitations associated with scalability, integration complexity, and phonon mismatch remain significant barriers for real‑world deployment.
articles.summary_en: The paper reviews graphene and other two-dimensional nanomaterials for thermal interface materials targeting rising heat densities in HPC and AI data centers. It finds enhanced thermal transport and interface engineering potential, while scalability, integration complexity, and phonon mismatch remain barriers to deployment.

articles.title_original: Fluorination of Bidimensional Materials
articles.title_en: Review Examines Fluorination Strategies for Graphene and Other 2D Materials
articles.excerpt_original: Fluorination has emerged as a powerful strategy for tailoring the structure, chemistry, and electronic properties of two-dimensional (2D) materials beyond conventional surface functionalization. This review highlights fluorination chemistry as a versatile toolbox for the controlled design of layered materials, with particular emphasis on synthesis approaches, reaction mechanisms, and structural transformations of graphene and carbon materials, hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN), transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), MXenes, layered double hydroxides (LDHs), and layered metal oxides. Various fluorination methods, including direct fluorination using F2, XeF2 treatment, HF-based processes, plasma-assisted fluorination, electrochemical routes, hydrothermal/solvothermal methods, and polymer-mediated topochemical fluorination, are critically discussed regarding their mechanisms, advantages, limitations, and ability to control fluorine content, bonding configuration, defect formation, and phase evolution. Finally, current challenges related to fluorine control, scalability, environmental impact, and advanced characterization are discussed. Fluorination–defluorination chemistry is thus presented as a promising platform for atomic-scale engineering of 2D materials.
articles.summary_en: A review evaluates fluorination methods for tailoring the structure, chemistry, and electronic properties of graphene and other layered materials. It compares reaction mechanisms, control of fluorine content and defects, scalability, environmental impacts, and characterization challenges.

articles.title_original: Displacement-Field-Induced Ionization of Defect States in High-Quality hBN
articles.title_en: Displacement Fields Ionize Defects in hBN-Encapsulated Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Encapsulation of two-dimensional (2D) materials with hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is widely used to fabricate ultraclean van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures for optoelectronic and quantum transport studies. These devices are often operated under strong out-of-plane displacement fields that tune the electronic properties of the active 2D material, while the surrounding hBN is typically assumed to remain electronically inert. This assumption, however, neglects defect states that are present even in high-quality hBN crystals. Here, we probe their response to the applied displacement field using monolayer graphene encapsulated between hBN crystals as a sensitive charge sensor. Increasing the displacement field induces notable charge transfer between graphene and hBN, producing additional electron doping of 10-20x10^9 cm^(-2) even at the moderate displacement field (~0.5 V nm^(-1)), while simultaneously increasing carrier-density inhomogeneity of the graphene layer. Both effects are consistent with ionization of defect states within the hBN bandgap, with the bulk density ~1-7x10^(-5) nm^(-3) varying across different hBN crystals. Our results show that displacement-field-induced defect ionization in hBN can modify the electronic response of vdW heterostructures, with direct implications for device design and interpretation of experiments.
articles.summary_en: Researchers show that moderate out-of-plane displacement fields can ionize defect states in supposedly inert hBN, transferring charge to encapsulated graphene and increasing carrier-density inhomogeneity. The findings have direct implications for the design and interpretation of van der Waals semiconductor and quantum-transport devices.

articles.title_original: 2D Quantum Materials
articles.title_en: Review Maps 2D Materials for Next-Generation Photodetectors
articles.excerpt_original: The discovery of graphene in 2004 catalyzed a global shift in optoelectronics, demonstrating that atomically thin materials could deliver electronic and optical performance previously unattainable in conventional bulk semiconductors. Since then, a wide range of two-dimensional (2D) materials have emerged, including transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), black phosphorus (BP), transition-metal carbides (MXenes), hexagonal boron nitride, and emerging van der Waals heterostructures. These materials offer tunable bandgaps, two strong light–matter interactions, mechanical flexibility, and compatibility with heterogeneous integration. These intrinsic advantages have positioned 2D materials as compelling platforms for next-generation photodetectors spanning ultraviolet to terahertz regimes. This chapter surveys the evolution of 2D photodetectors from graphene&s;s broadband but low-responsivity prototypes to engineered architectures exploiting bandgap engineering, interlayer charge transfer, plasmonic enhancement, and hybrid organic–inorganic coupling. Material systems, device geometries, and performance metrics are compared with emphasis on reproducibility, stability, and integration pathways relevant to scalable manufacturing. By mapping strengths and limitations across 2D platforms, the chapter provides a sponsor-defensible framework for selecting and engineering photodetectors tailored to specific spectral bands, noise constraints, and system-level requirements.
articles.summary_en: This academic chapter surveys graphene, transition-metal dichalcogenides, black phosphorus, MXenes, hexagonal boron nitride, and van der Waals heterostructures for photodetection from ultraviolet to terahertz wavelengths. It compares material systems, device architectures, performance metrics, and manufacturing-integration challenges, highlighting bandgap engineering and hybrid approaches beyond graphene’s broadband but low-responsivity prototypes.

articles.title_original: Low-loading Ni/h-BN catalysts for low-temperature selective semi-hydrogenation of 1,3-butadiene to butenes: Mechanistic Insights from in situ and transient DRIFTS
articles.title_en: Low-loading nickel/h-BN catalysts improve low-temperature butadiene hydrogenation
articles.excerpt_original: Selective hydrogenation of 1,3-butadiene to butenes at low temperatures is challenged by consecutive hydrogenation of the desired products to butane. Here, a series of xNi/h-BN catalysts with Ni loadings of 0.25–1.0 wt% was prepared by impregnation to investigate loading-dependent catalytic behavior. The h-BN-supported catalyst exhibited substantially higher low-temperature conversion than its Al 2 O 3 -supported counterpart at the same nominal Ni loading. Increasing Ni loading enhanced 1,3-butadiene conversion but decreased total butene selectivity, revealing an activity–selectivity trade-off. Notably, 0.25Ni/h-BN achieved a butene yield of 60.7% with 92.2% selectivity at 70 °C, whereas 0.5Ni/h-BN delivered a comparable yield of 59.1% at 60 °C. TEM, H 2 -TPR, and XPS revealed loading-dependent changes in Ni particle size, reducibility, and surface speciation. In situ CO-DRIFTS showed less persistent CO retention over 0.25Ni/h-BN and 0.5Ni/h-BN than over the higher-loading catalysts. Transient DRIFTS further supported the adsorption and subsequent transformation of butadiene-derived unsaturated species upon H 2 introduction. Together, these results suggest that adsorbate retention and possible readsorption contribute to the stronger over-hydrogenation tendency at higher Ni loading. This work highlights the importance of balancing reactant conversion with product release in developing non-noble-metal catalysts for low-temperature selective diene hydrogenation.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed nickel-supported hexagonal boron nitride catalysts that achieved up to 60.7% butene yield with 92.2% selectivity at 70 °C. The study links performance and over-hydrogenation to nickel loading, particle size, reducibility, and adsorbate retention.

articles.title_original: Multifunctionality in Janus CrMCN4 (M = Si/Ge) Monolayers: Valleytronic Physics, Piezoelectric Response, and Photocatalytic Potential
articles.title_en: Janus CrSiCN4 and CrGeCN4 Monolayers Show Tunable Valleytronic and Piezoelectric Properties
articles.excerpt_original: Two dimensional Janus semiconductors integrating spin-valley coupling, piezoelectricity, and tunable optical responses offer a platform for multifunctional nanodevices. Here, first-principles calculations reveal complementary composition and strain effects in CrSiCN4 and CrGeCN4 monolayers. Both are found to be nonmagnetic direct-gap semiconductors, with gaps of 1.23 and 1.09 eV using the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof functional including spin-orbit coupling, respectively. HSE06 hybrid-functional calculations retain the direct-gap character, yielding gaps of 1.46 eV for CrSiCN4 and 1.19 eV for CrGeCN4. Opposite out-of-plane spin character and Berry curvature emerge at K and K'. Biaxial strain reduces the respective gaps from 1.59 to 0.86 eV and 1.44 to 0.63 eV, drives direct-to-indirect transitions, and redshifts absorption while preserving valley spin contrast. CrGeCN4 exhibits larger in-plane piezoelectric response, whereas CrSiCN4 exhibits larger out-of-plane magnitude. Band-edge alignment satisfies the oxygen evolution reaction requirement but provides insufficient driving force for the hydrogen evolution reaction, motivating further strain-induced band-edge modulation toward overall water splitting. These results establish composition and strain as complementary controls for tailoring Cr-based Janus monolayers for valleytronic, optoelectronic, electromechanical, and photocatalytic applications.
articles.summary_en: First-principles calculations identify CrSiCN4 and CrGeCN4 as direct-gap semiconductors with strain-tunable electronic, optical, valleytronic, and piezoelectric responses. Their band alignment supports oxygen evolution but not hydrogen evolution, indicating photocatalytic promise that requires further engineering for complete water splitting.

articles.title_original: Synthesis and Advanced Characterization Techniques
articles.title_en: Review Surveys Synthesis and Characterization of 2D Quantum Materials
articles.excerpt_original: Two-dimensional (2D) quantum materials provide a versatile platform for exploring emergent electronic, optical, and energy-related phenomena arising from strong structure–property coupling. Their atomically thin nature enables precise control over defects, interfaces, strain, and layer stacking configurations, allowing quantum states to be created and engineered through material processes. Reliable synthesis methods and nanoscale characterization techniques are central to the development of functional 2D material systems hosting quantum phenomena. This chapter reviews key synthesis strategies and characterization approaches for 2D quantum materials. We first discuss representative synthesis methods that offer different advantages in crystallinity, scalability, and stoichiometric control, which strongly influence device performance. Next, we summarize advanced characterization techniques used to probe atomic structure, electronic environments, strain distributions, and excitonic behavior. Finally, representative platforms, including hexagonal boron nitride, transition metal dichalcogenides, topological quantum materials, and 2D magnetic materials, are discussed to illustrate how synthesis and nanoscale characterization enable investigation of defect engineering, strain modulation, and heterostructure design for quantum and energy-related technologies.
articles.summary_en: This academic chapter reviews synthesis strategies and nanoscale characterization methods for two-dimensional quantum materials. It covers hexagonal boron nitride, transition metal dichalcogenides, topological quantum materials, and 2D magnetic materials in contexts including quantum, semiconductor, and energy-related technologies.

articles.title_original: Controlling spin relaxation in 2D hybrid organic-inorganic semiconductors
articles.title_en: Engineering Spin Relaxation in 2D Hybrid Perovskites
articles.excerpt_original: Two-dimensional hybrid organic-inorganic perovskites (2D HOIPs) have emerged as a promising class of semiconductors for next-generation spin-optoelectronic applications, owing to their structural tunability and rich spin-dependent optoelectronic properties. Their layered organic-inorganic architectures also offer opportunities to control spin relaxation via chirality, layer-number tuning, and symmetry engineering. This work discusses how 2D HOIPs can be engineered to manipulate spin dynamics. The first part focuses on quasi-2D chiral perovskites, in which we vary the layer number and uncover how structural confinement governs chiroptical response, spin relaxation, and charge-carrier mobility. The second part highlights inversion-symmetric 2D perovskites, in which local symmetry breaking within the inorganic layers leads to hidden spin-valley locking via functional non-primary ammonium cations. This local structural asymmetry produces large spin splitting and spin-valley textures, which protect optically generated spin-polarized carriers and reveal room temperature spin lifetimes of hundreds of picoseconds in the Pb-based system.
articles.summary_en: Research shows that chirality, layer-number control, and symmetry engineering can tune spin relaxation and charge-carrier mobility in two-dimensional hybrid organic–inorganic perovskites. Local structural asymmetry also produces spin-valley locking and room-temperature spin lifetimes of hundreds of picoseconds in lead-based systems, supporting spin-optoelectronic applications.

articles.title_original: Two-Dimensional Materials for Wide-Bandgap and Ultrawide-Bandgap Semiconductor Integration: Epitaxy, Interfaces, and Optoelectronic Devices
articles.title_en: 2D Materials Enable Integration of Wide-Bandgap Semiconductors
articles.excerpt_original: Wide-bandgap (WBG) and ultrawide-bandgap (UWBG) semiconductors are key materials for high-power electronics, radio-frequency electronics, and ultraviolet optoelectronics. However, heterogeneous integration remains challenging because conventional heteroepitaxy is constrained by lattice mismatch and differences in thermal expansion coefficients, while interface states and non-ideal metal–semiconductor contacts can degrade carrier transport and device performance. Two-dimensional (2D) materials offer an important alternative approach to heterogeneous integration. Their dangling-bond-free surfaces and van der Waals interactions relax lattice-matching requirements and facilitate membrane release, while their tunable electronic properties enable control over band alignment and interfacial carrier transport. This review examines the integration of 2D materials with WBG and UWBG semiconductors, focusing on epitaxial growth, interface physics, optoelectronic devices, and scalable integration. Representative 2D material-assisted epitaxial modes include remote, pinhole, and van der Waals epitaxy. Mixed-dimensional heterostructures are discussed in terms of their interfacial electronic properties, contact engineering, passivation strategies, and thermal transport. Photodetection represents an important optoelectronic application of these heterostructures. Taken together, these advances highlight the growing importance of 2D materials in WBG and UWBG integration and point to broader opportunities in future electronics.
articles.summary_en: A review examines how two-dimensional materials address lattice mismatch, interface states, and contact limitations in wide-bandgap and ultrawide-bandgap semiconductor integration. It highlights van der Waals epitaxy, interface engineering, passivation, thermal transport, and photodetection as routes toward scalable optoelectronic devices.

articles.title_original: D2.3 Graphene-enhanced structural supercapacitor electrodes
articles.title_en: Graphene-Functionalized Carbon-Fiber Electrodes for Structural Supercapacitors
articles.excerpt_original: The purpose of this deliverable is to report the research carried out on the development of carbon fiber (CF) electrodes within Task 2.2 (WP2), aimed at enhancing their electrochemical performance. Briefly, initially commercial CF fabrics were modified through desizing and activation. Then three surface functionalization strategies based on Graphene, MXenes and activated carbon were investigated to improve the capacitance of CF for their use as structural supercapacitor electrodes (WP5). The deliverable establishes methodologies for CF functionalization and electrochemical characterization, including a validated three-electrode testing protocol for consistent electrode evaluation.
articles.summary_en: The deliverable investigates graphene, MXene, and activated-carbon surface treatments for improving the capacitance of carbon-fiber fabrics used as structural supercapacitor electrodes. It also establishes functionalization methods and a validated three-electrode testing protocol for electrochemical evaluation.

articles.title_original: Wafer-scale low-symmetry graphene moiré superlattice for integrated quantum rectifiers
articles.title_en: Wafer-scale graphene enables CMOS-compatible quantum rectifiers
articles.excerpt_original: Low-symmetry materials unlock rich Berry curvature physics and anomalous transport phenomena that are forbidden in high-symmetry quantum systems through rigorous crystalline symmetry constraints. Current approaches rely on external fields or complex heterogeneous stacking to break crystalline symmetries, which hinders scalable device integration. In this work, we demonstrate surface premelting engineering to create wafer-scale low-symmetry graphene on germanium-110 [Ge(110)]. Controlled premelting forms striped germanium surface patterns that reduce graphene symmetry from D 6h to C 1v , producing a room-temperature nonlinear Hall conductivity of ~11 micrometers per volt per ohm. First-principles calculations attribute this to originating from overtilted massive Dirac cones of hybridized germanium bands and the graphene Dirac cone. Integrated nonlinear Hall rectifiers generate >20 millivolts of output from radio frequency input and drive commercial voltage boosters and light-emitting diodes, establishing a complementary metal-oxide semiconductor–compatible route toward wafer-scale nonlinear quantum devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers created low-symmetry graphene on germanium wafers using surface premelting, producing room-temperature nonlinear Hall conductivity. Integrated rectifiers generated more than 20 mV from radio-frequency input and powered commercial voltage boosters and LEDs, indicating potential for scalable quantum-device integration.

articles.title_original: Strain engineering of Hf2CO2 MXene for enhanced transport and photoresponse in nanodevices
articles.title_en: Strain engineering boosts Hf₂CO₂ MXene transport and photoresponse
articles.excerpt_original: MXenes have emerged as promising semiconductor materials for applications in nanoelectronics and optoelectronics. In this study, Hf 2 CO 2 MXene was systematically investigated to elucidate its intrinsic material properties, quantum transport behavior, and photoelectric response mechanisms. The Hf 2 CO 2 monolayer was identified as a stable semiconductor with a bandgap of 1.57 eV. Notably, this bandgap was modulated under biaxial tensile strain, increasing to 1.83 eV under 4 % strain and to 1.94 eV under 8 % strain. This material is predicted to retain dynamic, thermal, and mechanical stability throughout strain application. Additionally, strain engineering significantly enhanced device performance: the current density of the p–n junction diode reached 47 mA/mm, while the p–i–n junction field-effect transistor achieved a maximum current density of 1000 mA/mm at a gate voltage of − 4 V under 8 % strain. In terms of the photoresponse, Hf 2 CO 2 exhibited distinct absorption peaks in the green–blue and ultraviolet regions. Under strain modulation, the intrinsic photocurrent density of the phototransistor reached 1.2 mA/mm 2 , highlighting its potential for broadband photodetection and photovoltaic applications.
articles.summary_en: An academic study models Hf₂CO₂ MXene as a stable semiconductor whose bandgap and device performance increase under biaxial tensile strain. At 8% strain, predicted current densities reached 1,000 mA/mm in a p–i–n field-effect transistor and 1.2 mA/mm² in a phototransistor, indicating potential for nanoelectronics, photodetection, and photovoltaic applications.

articles.title_original: PAN/PI-Derived Carbon Nanofibrous Membranes with MXene-Assisted Contact Modulation for Heat-Resistant Piezoresistive Sensing and Thermal Warning Response
articles.title_en: MXene-Assisted Carbon Nanofiber Membrane Enables Heat-Resistant Pressure Sensing
articles.excerpt_original: Flexible piezoresistive sensors for protective textiles should maintain pressure-responsive conductivity after thermal exposure, whereas many polymer-based sensing layers soften, degrade, or lose signal output under heat. Herein, we report a self-supporting PAN/PI-derived carbon nanofibrous membrane with MXene-assisted contact modulation for heat-resistant piezoresistive sensing and temperature-triggered warning. Electrospun PAN/PAA membranes were stabilized and carbonized to construct a thermally durable conductive fibrous framework, in which PAN serves as the principal carbon-forming precursor and the PAA-derived PI intermediate assists structural retention during thermal conversion. Surface-deposited Ti3C2Tx MXene nanosheets further introduce conductive junctions and pressure-responsive contact interfaces. The optimized PPNF-MX3 sensor exhibits a broad pressure range of 0.05-250 kPa, a low-pressure sensitivity of 8.16 kPa-1, and response/recovery times of 520/572 ms. It retains 97.51% of its electromechanical response after 10,000 bending-release cycles at room temperature and 83.16% after 1200 cycles following thermal exposure at 350 °C for 660 s. The carbonized membrane exhibits thermal-shielding behavior and flame-induced structural retention, while the integrated system enables repeatable temperature-triggered warning at 495 °C. These results demonstrate the potential of PPNF-MX3 as a multifunctional sensing and thermal-warning platform for intelligent protective textiles exposed to demanding thermal environments.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a PAN/PI-derived carbon nanofibrous membrane with Ti3C2Tx MXene conductive junctions for piezoresistive sensing and thermal warnings. The sensor retained 83.16% of its electromechanical response after exposure cycling at 350 °C and generated warnings at 495 °C, supporting protective-textile applications.

articles.title_original: Research Progress in Quantum Precision Measurement of Hexagonal Boron Nitride Color Centers
articles.title_en: Review Advances in Quantum Precision Sensing with Hexagonal Boron Nitride Color Centers
articles.excerpt_original: 作为广泛使用的二维材料，六方氮化硼在凝聚态物理、量子器件等领域研究中发挥着重要作用。近年来，基于六方氮化硼色心的量子精密测量技术受到了广泛的关注——这类固态量子传感器具备微米级空间分辨率、高探测灵敏度以及优异的原位探测能力，尤其适用于量子器件的微区物性测量研究.本文系统梳理了六方氮化硼中典型色心结构，包括负电硼空位色心和碳相关色心的制备工艺与物理特性；并以二维磁性材料磁成像、温度传感、应变测量及高压原位压力探测为例，介绍了六方氮化硼色心在多物理量精密测量中的研究进展.本文还讨论了通过光子学结构增强、自旋操控序列优化、同位素纯化等方法进一步提高六方氮化硼色心传感性能的方案，以期为二维材料色心量子精密测量技术的发展和应用提供参考.
articles.summary_en: The review examines hexagonal boron nitride color centers, including negatively charged boron vacancies and carbon-related centers, for solid-state quantum sensing. It covers magnetic imaging, temperature, strain, and in-situ high-pressure measurements, along with approaches to improve performance through photonic enhancement, spin-control optimization, and isotope purification.

articles.title_original: Switchable Electroosmotic Delivery via Capillary Shrunken Reduced Graphene Oxide Membrane
articles.title_en: Switchable Electroosmotic Delivery Enabled by Shrunken Reduced Graphene Oxide Membranes
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract A capillary-force-assisted reduced graphene oxide (rGO) membrane is developed for electrically controlled electroosmotic flow (EOF). By combining capillary drying with subsequent freeze-drying, structural shrinkage is used to continuously control the pore size and channel density of the membrane. The resulting membrane shows enhanced EOF together with switchable transport behavior enabled by electrical parameter regulation. Under the optimized 20 h capillary drying condition, the membrane exhibits an EOF intensity of about 1.15 μL min−1 cm−2 and enables symmetric four-mode electrical switching of EOF direction and intensity through independent regulation of driving current and membrane-bias polarity. This switchable EOF is further translated into switchable molecular delivery, allowing reversible regulation of glucose and FITC-dextran (MW: 10 kDa) transport between opposite directions; in the transport-favorable direction, the transported amounts are 3.23 and 5.06× higher, respectively, than those in the opposite direction. Together, these results provide a practical route for flexible electroosmotic systems requiring electrically switchable and reversible molecular transport.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a capillary-shrunken reduced graphene oxide membrane with electrically switchable electroosmotic flow. The system reversibly controls glucose and dextran transport direction and intensity, suggesting applications in programmable molecular-delivery systems.

articles.title_original: Chip-Scale Plasma-Sulfurized Nanocrystalline MoS2-Graphene Heterostructure-Based Optoelectronic Synaptic Transistor
articles.title_en: Chip-Scale MoS₂–Graphene Synaptic Transistor Enables UV-Selective Neuromorphic Sensing
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Optoelectronic synaptic devices based on 2D van der Waals (vdW) materials are very promising for next-generation, energy-efficient data processing and sensing; however, flake-based fabrication limits their practical application. Here, scalable inductively coupled plasma-sulfurized nanocrystalline MoS2 (nc-MoS2) and graphene heterostructure have been investigated for optoelectronic synaptic device applications. The nc-MoS2 with abundant sulfur vacancies, grain boundaries, and defect states facilitates charge trapping at the nc-MoS2/Graphene interface and introduces negative persistent photocurrent (PPC). The PPC state is effective only for ultraviolet (UV) light because of the high recombination of photogenerated charge carriers at the defect sites of nc-MoS2 for higher wavelength light; however, it enables energy-efficient, neuromorphic UV-selective sensing that could serve as a UV exposure alert system. The device demonstrates efficient emulation of fundamental synaptic behaviors, including short-term memory, long-term memory, and paired-pulse facilitation, through modulation of optical stimuli such as light intensity and illumination duration, as well as reconfiguration via the gate voltage. A 96.94% accuracy in MINST image recognition has also been demonstrated through deep neural network-based simulation, which seems potentially applicable in neuromorphic computing. Thus, the nc-MoS2/Gr heterostructure, as a scalable, 2D vdW system, has significant potential for optoelectronic synapses.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a scalable plasma-sulfurized nanocrystalline MoS₂–graphene heterostructure that emulates synaptic behaviors and selectively responds to ultraviolet light. The device achieved 96.94% simulated image-recognition accuracy, indicating potential for energy-efficient UV alerts and neuromorphic computing.

articles.title_original: Resonance-Tuned Plasmon–Phonon Hybridization in Continuous Bilayer Graphene
articles.title_en: Resonance-Tuned Plasmon–Phonon Hybridization Demonstrated in Bilayer Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Bilayer graphene hosts an infrared-active antisymmetric (Eu) optical phonon whose spectral response is strongly influenced by electronic excitations. While carrier-density control of this phonon has been widely studied, its interaction with collective electronic excitations, graphene plasmons, at nominally fixed carrier density remains less explored. Here we show that resonant plasmonic excitation in chemically doped AB-stacked BLG reshapes the optical phonon response through plasmon–phonon hybridization. A grating-coupled resonator enables efficient far-field excitation of plasmons in a continuous BLG sheet, while a built-in photonic cavity modulates the plasmonic resonance strength. We observe systematic changes in Fano asymmetry, apparent resonance position, spectral weight, and effective line width near the plasmon-strength maximum. Correlation analysis and numerical simulations support plasmon–phonon hybridization as the dominant origin of the observed spectral evolution, with possible intrinsic phonon–electronic coupling. Our findings identify resonance tuning as a distinct route to control plasmon–phonon hybridization and engineer nanoscale mid-infrared light–matter interactions.
articles.summary_en: Researchers show that resonant plasmonic excitation can reshape optical phonon responses in chemically doped bilayer graphene at fixed carrier density. The findings establish resonance tuning as a route to engineer nanoscale mid-infrared light–matter interactions.

articles.title_original: Thermally Regulated HOF-101/MXene-Driven PEC/ECL Dual-Mode Molecularly Imprinted Sensor for Sensitive Detection of Nitrofurazone
articles.title_en: Thermally Regulated HOF-101/MXene Sensor Detects Nitrofurazone in Water
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The great promise of hydrogen-bonded organic frameworks (HOFs) in photoelectrochemical (PEC) and electrochemiluminescence (ECL) sensing is restricted by poor stability and low sensitivity. In this study, thermal regulation is employed to adjust the molecular packing and framework connectivity of HOF-101. The annealed HOF-101 with a fundamental periodic framework can provide a pronounced photocurrent response. Consequently, a mode-adapted HOF-101/MXene is employed in the dual-mode PEC/ECL molecularly imprinted sensor, enabling sensitive and reliable detection of nitrofurazone (NFZ), a nitrofuran antibiotic of significant regulatory concern. MXene functions either as an efficient charge-transport support to suppress photogenerated charge recombination and accelerate the interfacial reaction, or as an efficient coreactant accelerator to promote the redox kinetics of HOF-101 to boost its ECL emission. Thanks to stable and reliable dual-mode readout, the proposed sensor has a wide linear range of 1.0 × 10−1−1.0 × 105 ng mL−1 in PEC mode and 1.0 × 100−1.0 × 105 ng mL−1 in ECL mode, with a detection limit of 3.7 × 10−2 ng mL−1 and 2.3 × 10−2 ng mL−1, respectively. The sensor demonstrates good selectivity and satisfactory recoveries in river water samples. This work presents a potential platform for determining NFZs in environmental water monitoring and offers new insights into the thermally induced structural regulation of HOFs-based heterostructures for high-performance PEC/ECL sensing.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a dual-mode photoelectrochemical/electrochemiluminescence molecularly imprinted sensor using thermally regulated HOF-101 and MXene for sensitive nitrofurazone detection. The platform achieved sub-ng/mL detection limits and demonstrated selective recovery in river-water samples, supporting environmental monitoring applications.

articles.title_original: Interfacial engineering of graphene oxide immobilization on polylactic acid substrates through surface modification
articles.title_en: Surface-Engineered Graphene Oxide–PLA Composite Enables Reusable Dye Adsorption
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Graphene oxide (GO) exhibits strong adsorption capability for dye removal, but its practical utilization remains constrained by aggregation and poor recoverability in aqueous systems. In this study, GO was immobilized onto biodegradable polylactic acid (PLA) through an interfacial engineering strategy. PLA substrates were first activated by alkaline etching to increase surface roughness and energy, followed by 3‑aminopropyltriethoxysilane (KH550) silanization to enhance interfacial adhesion. GO was then deposited onto the modified PLA via ultrasonic-assisted coating. The as-prepared composite was systematically characterized using SEM, FTIR, Raman spectroscopy, and XRD, confirming successful GO immobilization. Stability tests demonstrated that the composite retained 93.7% and 81.5% of its initial GO loading in aqueous and acidic environments after 13 days, respectively. Methylene blue (MB) adsorption experiments revealed kinetics following the pseudo-second-order model with adsorption equilibrium reached within approximately 60 min. The adsorption data were well described by the Langmuir isotherm model, yielding a maximum adsorption capacity of 197.21 mg·g −1 , indicative of monolayer adsorption. After six adsorption–desorption cycles, the composite retained 75.2% of its initial adsorption capacity, indicating satisfactory reusability. This work developed a surface-engineered GO–PLA composite through an effective surface modification strategy, generating a stable and reusable material whose functional performance was validated by the adsorption experiments.
articles.summary_en: Researchers immobilized graphene oxide on alkaline-etched and silanized polylactic acid, improving aqueous stability and preventing aggregation. The composite adsorbed methylene blue at up to 197.21 mg·g−1 and retained 75.2% of its capacity after six cycles, supporting potential use in reusable water-treatment materials.

articles.title_original: Plasma Processing of Graphene and Related 2D Materials
articles.title_en: Plasma Processing Advances for Graphene and 2D Materials
articles.excerpt_original: Graphene and related two-dimensional (2D) materials exhibit exceptional electrical, mechanical, optical, and chemical properties owing to their atomically thin structure, strong in-plane bonding, and weak van der Waals interactions. Beyond graphene, materials such as hexagonal boron nitride (hBN), black phosphorus (BP), transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs), and MXenes show strong potential for next-generation electronics, optoelectronics, and energy systems. This chapter discusses the fundamentals and applications of plasma processing in 2D materials. The basics of plasma-surface interactions are introduced to support understanding of plasma-assisted modifications. Advantages such as low-temperature operation, high chemical reactivity, and precise surface control are highlighted. Particular attention is given to plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD) for large-area growth of hBN, TMDCs, BP, and their heterostructures, along with plasma-chemistry-driven tuning of electrical, optical, magnetic, and chemical/structural properties.
articles.summary_en: This research chapter reviews plasma-based modification and growth of graphene and related 2D materials, emphasizing low-temperature processing, high chemical reactivity, and precise surface control. It highlights PECVD and plasma chemistry for tuning properties relevant to electronics, optoelectronics, and energy systems.

articles.excerpt_original: Abstract A tough interconnected dual conductive network was constructed in cement mortar through the synergistic incorporation of one-dimensional multiwalled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs), two-dimensional MXene nanosheets, and carboxylated cellulose nanofibers (CNFs). To minimize nanoparticle agglomeration and improve conductive-network continuity, a combined strategy integrating ultrasonic predispersion, in situ directional assembly, and vacuum-assisted incorporation was adopted to regulate the spatial organization of conductive nanocomponents within the cementitious matrix. The effects of different component dosages on electrical resistivity, stress sensitivity coefficient, mechanical properties, and microstructural evolution were systematically investigated. The results showed that the incorporation of MXene significantly optimized the conductive-network topology and reduced the percolation threshold of the ternary system to 1.76 × 10–4, corresponding to a 63.2% decrease compared with the single-MWCNTs system. Among all groups, T30F30M25 exhibited the best electromechanical synergy, with a 27.58% reduction in resistivity, a stress sensitivity coefficient of 0.081%/MPa, and increases of 27.51% and 60.59% in compressive and flexural strengths, respectively, relative to the control group. Multiscale characterizations demonstrated that MXene promoted AFt and C–S–H gel formation and refined CH crystallites, while MWCNTs provided crack-bridging pathways and CNFs improved conductive-network continuity through steric hindrance and interfacial regulation. articles.summary_en: Researchers developed cement mortar containing MWCNTs, MXene nanosheets and cellulose nanofibers, forming a stable conductive network for electromechanical sensing. articles.title_original: MOF-derived oxygen-vacancy-rich CeO2-C/single-layered MXene composites for the individual and simultaneous detection of dopamine and uric acid in serum and urine
articles.title_en: MXene–CeO₂-C Sensor Detects Dopamine and Uric Acid in Biofluids
articles.excerpt_original: Constructing a sensing interface that integrates high catalytic activity with excellent conductivity is crucial for enhancing the performance of electrochemical analysis in complex biological systems. In this study, a novel electrochemical sensing platform was successfully constructed via the synergistic assembly of cerium-based metal-organic framework (MOF)-derived porous CeO 2 -C composites and single-layered MXene (SL-MXene), which enables the sensitive individual and simultaneous detection of dopamine (DA) and uric acid (UA). The CeO 2 -C nanoparticles, rich in oxygen vacancies, provide abundant catalytically active sites and significantly enhance the enrichment and redox catalytic capability toward DA and UA. Meanwhile, the SL-MXene nanosheets, featuring a large specific surface area and outstanding electrical conductivity, serve as an efficient electron transfer medium that effectively promotes charge transfer at the electrode interface. The synergistic coupling of the two components not only amplifies the electrochemical response signals but also endows the sensor with the ability to resolve the distinct oxidation potential differences between DA and UA. Under optimal conditions, the sensor exhibits excellent linear responses for both DA and UA over a wide concentration range of 1–300 μM, with detection limits as low as 0.07 μM and 0.04 μM for simultaneous detection, respectively. Furthermore, the sensor demonstrates favorable anti-interference capability, repeatability, and long-term stability, and has been successfully applied to the quantitative analysis of DA and UA in human serum and urine samples, with recovery rates ranging from 95.8% to 105.0% for DA and 98.4% to 104.1% for UA in serum, and from 97.2% to 105.4% for DA and 98.8% to 101.4% for UA in urine.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed an electrochemical sensor combining oxygen-vacancy-rich CeO₂-C nanoparticles with single-layer MXene for individual and simultaneous detection of dopamine and uric acid. articles.title_original: Photonic thermal management of overhead cables via high-thermal-conductivity radiative cooling
articles.title_en: h-BN Radiative-Cooling Coating Raises Overhead Cable Ampacity
articles.excerpt_original: As the thermal backbone of urban energy infrastructure, transmission cables directly affect the stability and resilience of modern cities. However, high operating temperatures, driven by Joule heating and solar radiation, critically limit the ampacity of overhead transmission lines, particularly under extreme climate conditions. Such high temperatures constrain electricity delivery and pose systemic risks to essential services and long-term urban sustainability. To overcome this challenge, we adopt a high thermal conductivity radiative cooling (HTCRC) coating comprising hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) nanoparticles embedded in a polydimethylsiloxane matrix to reduce cable temperature. Enabled by photonic thermal management, this composite structure simultaneously achieves high solar reflectance (0.92) through efficient light scattering, strong mid-infrared emissivity via polymer vibrational modes (0.95), and enhanced thermal conductivity (1.28 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹). Outdoor experiments demonstrate notable daytime cooling of simulated HTCRC-coated power cables, maintaining safe operating temperatures even under intense solar exposure. In addition, thermal modeling based on the CIGRE 601 standard reveals a 6-10% increase in ampacity across representative hot-climate cities globally. These findings highlight high thermal conductivity radiative cooling as an effective and scalable strategy to enhance urban power grid performance, improve energy delivery security, and support the development of climate-resilient cities under rapidly growing electricity demand driven by electrification and the expanding energy footprint of artificial intelligence.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a hexagonal boron nitride–polydimethylsiloxane coating that combines high solar reflectance, infrared emissivity, and thermal conductivity to cool overhead power cables. Outdoor tests and CIGRE-based modeling indicated safe-temperature operation and a 6–10% ampacity increase in hot climates.

articles.title_original: The energetics of high temperature oxidation and formation mechanisms in binary lanthanide nitrides (LnN)
articles.title_en: Thermodynamics of Lanthanide Nitride Oxidation Relevant to Nuclear Fuel Management
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Nitride-based materials present exceptional thermal and structural properties for advanced material applications, however accurate determination of their thermodynamic properties is critical to their deployment. Herein, the standard enthalpies of formation, Δ H f ° , for all Ln N compounds ( Ln = La, Ce, Pr, Nd, Sm, Eu, Gd, Tb, Dy, Ho, Er, Tm, Lu; excluding Pm) are determined via high temperature oxide melt calorimetry. These measurements are supported by high temperature oxidation studies of La, Ce, Sm, Eu, Er, Yb bearing Ln N compounds using X-ray diffraction and thermogravimetric analysis, and are cross-examined against recent high temperature measurements on other Ln N compounds 1 . It was determined that Δ H f ° systematically correlates with the ionic radius of Ln 3+ cations, with smaller Ln bearing nitrides having more negative values. A discontinuity in Δ H f ° was further observed between larger and smaller Ln bearing Ln N compounds. Using the determined Δ H f ° values with literature references, Gibbs energies of formation (Δ G f ° ), oxidation (Δ G ox ° ) and hydrolysis (Δ G hyd ° ) are calculated and compared against uranium nitride (UN) in the context of UN based nuclear fuel and related spent nuclear fuel (SNF) management. The calculations indicate that the occurrence of Ln N phases within UN based SNF should lead to stabilisation of the structure and inhibit its oxidation.
articles.summary_en: Researchers measured formation enthalpies and oxidation behavior for lanthanide nitrides, finding systematic dependence on lanthanide ionic radius.
